24-def Aexp.Equiv (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : Prop :=
25-  ∀ (st : State),
26-    a₁.eval st = a₂.eval st
27-
28-theorem Aexp.equiv_def {a₁ a₂ : Aexp} :
29-    a₁.Equiv a₂ ↔ ∀ (st : State), a₁.eval st = a₂.eval st := by rfl
30-
31-def Bexp.Equiv (b₁ b₂ : Bexp) : Prop :=
32-  ∀ (st : State),
33-    b₁.eval st = b₂.eval st
34-
35-theorem Bexp.equiv_def {b₁ b₂ : Bexp} :
36-    b₁.Equiv b₂ ↔ ∀ (st : State), b₁.eval st = b₂.eval st := by rfl
37-
38-example : Aexp.Equiv
39-    (aexp { X - X })
40-    (aexp { 0 }) := by
41-  rw [Aexp.equiv_def]
42-  intro st
43-  simp
44-
45-example : Bexp.Equiv
46-    (bexp { X - X = 0 })
47-    (bexp { true }) := by
48-  rw [Bexp.equiv_def]
49-  intro st
50-  simp
51-
52-def Com.Equiv (c₁ c₂ : Com) : Prop :=
53-    ∀ {st st' : State},
54-      (st =[ c₁ ]=> st') ↔ (st =[ c₂ ]=> st')
55-
56-theorem Com.equiv_def {c₁ c₂ : Com} : c₁.Equiv c₂ ↔
57-    ∀ {st st' : State}, (st =[ c₁ ]=> st') ↔ (st =[ c₂ ]=> st') := by rfl

58-
59--- Our goal in this chapter is to develop the tools to work
60--- through some simple examples of *program verification* --
61--- i.e., to use the precise definition of Imp to prove formally
62--- that particular programs satisfy particular specifications
63--- of their behavior.
64-
65--- We'll develop a reasoning system called *Floyd-Hoare Logic*
66--- -- often shortened to just *Hoare Logic* -- in which each of
67--- the syntactic constructs of Imp is equipped with a generic
68--- "proof rule" that can be used to reason compositionally
69--- about the correctness of programs involving this construct.
70-
71--- Hoare Logic combines two beautiful ideas: a natural way of
72--- writing down *specifications* of programs, and a *structured
73--- proof technique* for proving that programs are correct with
74--- respect to such specifications -- where by "structured" we
75--- mean that the structure of proofs directly mirrors the
76--- structure of the programs that they are about.
77-
78--- Note to developers:
79---     `HIDE: MRC'20: The terse version used to start with just an outline of
80---     what we've done and of this chapter, but it never mentioned Hoare logic!
81---     The text above seems like a better intro.
82---
83---     MRC'20: this is the former terse intro.
84---
85---      What we've done so far:
86---
87---      - Formalized Imp
88---           - identifiers and states
89---           - abstract syntax trees
90---           - evaluation functions (for [aexp]s and [bexp]s)
91---           - evaluation relation (for commands)
92---
93---      - Proved some _metatheoretic_ properties
94---          - determinism of evaluation
95---          - equivalence of some different ways of writing down the
96---            definitions (e.g., functional and relational definitions of
97---            arithmetic expression evaluation)
98---          - guaranteed termination of certain classes of programs
99---          - meaning-preservation of some program transformations
100---          - behavioral equivalence of programs ([Equiv])
101---
102---      We've dealt with a few sorts of properties of Imp programs:
103---        - Termination
104---        - Nontermination
105---        - Equivalence
106---
107---      Topic:
108---        - A systematic method for reasoning about the _functional
109---          correctness_ of programs in Imp
110---
111---      Goals:
112---        - a natural notation for _program specifications_ and
113---        - a _compositional_ proof technique for program correctness
114---
115---      Plan:
116---        - specifications (assertions / Hoare triples)
117---        - proof rules
118---        - loop invariants
119---        - decorated programs
120---        - examples`
121-
122--- ## Assertions
123-
124--- An *assertion* is a logical claim about the state of a
125--- program's memory -- formally, a predicate of `State`s.
126-
127-open scoped Com MyGetElem
128-
129-abbrev Assertion := State → Prop
130-
131--- Note to developers:
132---     HIDE: MRC'20: pulled up these examples from the
133---     quiz/optional exercise so that there would be some
134---     modeling of the kinds of answers we expect.
135-
136--- For example,
137-
138--- - `fun st => st[X] = 3` holds for states `st` in which value
139---   of `X` is `3`,
140-
141--- - `fun st => True` hold for all states, and
142-
143--- - `fun st => False` holds for no states.
144-
145--- _Quiz:_
146-
147--- Paraphrase the following assertions in English (i.e., say
148--- which states satisfy them)
149-
150--- (A) `fun st => st[X] ≤ st[Y]`
151-
152--- (B) `fun st => st[X] = 3 ∨ st[X] ≤ st[Y]`
153-
154--- (C)
155--- `fun st => st[Z] * st[Z] ≤ st[X] ∧ ¬ ((st[Z] + 1) * (st[Z] + 1) ≤ st[X])`
156-
157--- ### Notations for Assertions
158-
159--- We'll use Lean's notation features to make assertions look
160--- as much like informal math as possible.
161-
162--- For example, instead of writing
163-
164---   fun st => st[X] = m
165-
166--- we'll usually write just
167-
168---   {{ X = m }}
169-

185---     From what I can tell, the reason the notations expand during

235---
236---     There is now a custom entry [assn] for defining the syntax of
237---     assertions.  Like the delimiters <{ }> used for Imp programs,
238---     we now also have {{ }} delimiters for use with Assertions.
239---
240---     Inside that scope, variables, arithmetic and boolean expressions,
241---     propositions, and function arguments are interpreted in the current
242---     state.  This replaces the need for [ap], [ap2], and explicit lifting
243---     markers.
244---
245---     A raw Lean assertion can also be written directly inside {{ }}.`

257-  match stx with
258-  | `(assn($st; $t:term)) =>
259-    let t ← elabTerm t none
260-    let ty ← Meta.inferType t
261-    -- if (← Meta.isDefEq ty (mkConst ``_root_.Ident)) then -- this incorrectly assigns metavariables
262-    if (ty.constName == ``_root_.Ident) then
263-      return mkApp6 (mkConst ``_root_.MyGetElem.getElem)
264-        (mkApp2 (mkConst ``TotalMap) (mkConst ``String) (mkConst ``Nat))
265-        (mkConst ``String)
266-        (mkConst ``Nat)
267-        (← Meta.synthInstance <| mkApp3 (mkConst ``_root_.MyGetElem)
268-          (mkApp2 (mkConst ``TotalMap) (mkConst ``String) (mkConst ``Nat))
269-          (mkConst ``String)
270-          (mkConst ``Nat))
271-        (← elabTerm st none) t
272-    if (ty.constName == ``_root_.Aexp) then -- Detect an embedded `Aexp` and turn it into `Aexp.eval st t`
273-      return (mkApp2 (mkConst ``Aexp.eval) (← elabTerm st none) t)
274-    else if (ty.constName == ``_root_.Bexp) then  -- Detect an embedded `Bexp` and turn it into `Bexp.eval st t`
275-      return (mkApp2 (mkConst ``Bexp.eval) (← elabTerm st none) t)
276-    else if ty.isMVar then -- This is a hack to guard against `Meta.isDefEq` assigning the type to be an `Assertion`
277-      return t
278-    else if (← Meta.isDefEq ty (mkConst ``_root_.Assertion)) then
279-      return mkApp t (← elabTerm st none)
280-    else

282-  | _ => throwUnsupportedSyntax

286-  | `({{ $t }}) => `((fun st : _root_.State => assn(st; $t) : Assertion))

288-macro_rules
289-  | `(assn($st; ($P))) => ``((assn($st; $P)))

291-  | `(assn($st; $l + $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) + assn($st; $r))
292-  | `(assn($st; $l - $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) - assn($st; $r))
293-  | `(assn($st; $l * $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) * assn($st; $r))
294-  | `(assn($st; $l ≤ $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) ≤ assn($st; $r))
295-  | `(assn($st; $l < $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) < assn($st; $r))
296-  | `(assn($st; $l ≥ $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) ≥ assn($st; $r))
297-  | `(assn($st; $l > $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) > assn($st; $r))
298-  | `(assn($st; $l ∧ $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) ∧ assn($st; $r))
299-  | `(assn($st; $l ∨ $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) ∨ assn($st; $r))
300-  | `(assn($st; $l → $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) → assn($st; $r))
301-  | `(assn($st; $l ↔ $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) ↔ assn($st; $r))
302-  | `(assn($st; ¬ $t)) => ``(¬ assn($st; $t))
303-  | `(assn($st; $f $args*)) => do
304-    let mut result := f
305-    for arg in args do
306-      result ← `($result assn($st; $arg))
307-    return result
308-end

392--- ### Printing Assertions
393-
394--- THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: printing assertions back
395-
396-namespace Assertion.Delab
397-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr Imp.Delab
398-
399-/-- Rebuild the surface form of an assertion body, undoing the state
400-threading the `assn` elaborator performs: `st[X]` prints as `X`,
401-`Aexp.eval st a` as `a`, `Bexp.eval st b = true` as `b`, an applied
402-assertion `P st` as `P`, and a subterm that does not mention the state
403-prints as itself. -/
404-partial def delabBody (stId : FVarId) : DelabM Term := do
405-  let e ← getExpr
406-  if !e.containsFVar stId then
407-    delab
408-  else
409-    match_expr e with
410-    | MyGetElem.getElem _ _ _ _ st _ =>
411-      guard (st == .fvar stId)
412-      withNaryArg 5 delab
413-    | Aexp.eval st _ =>
414-      guard (st == .fvar stId)
415-      withAppArg delab
416-    | HAdd.hAdd _ _ _ _ _ _ =>
417-      `($(← withNaryArg 4 (delabBody stId)) + $(← withNaryArg 5 (delabBody stId)))
418-    | HSub.hSub _ _ _ _ _ _ =>
419-      `($(← withNaryArg 4 (delabBody stId)) - $(← withNaryArg 5 (delabBody stId)))
420-    | HMul.hMul _ _ _ _ _ _ =>
421-      `($(← withNaryArg 4 (delabBody stId)) * $(← withNaryArg 5 (delabBody stId)))
422-    | Eq _ l r =>
423-      -- `Bexp.eval st b = true` is the threaded form of a bare boolean `b`
424-      if r.isConstOf ``Bool.true && l.isAppOfArity ``Bexp.eval 2
425-          && l.appFn!.appArg! == .fvar stId then
426-        withNaryArg 1 <| withAppArg delab
427-      else
428-        `($(← withNaryArg 1 (delabBody stId)) = $(← withNaryArg 2 (delabBody stId)))
429-    | Ne _ _ _ =>
430-      `($(← withNaryArg 1 (delabBody stId)) ≠ $(← withNaryArg 2 (delabBody stId)))
431-    | LE.le _ _ _ _ =>
432-      `($(← withNaryArg 2 (delabBody stId)) ≤ $(← withNaryArg 3 (delabBody stId)))
433-    | LT.lt _ _ _ _ =>
434-      `($(← withNaryArg 2 (delabBody stId)) < $(← withNaryArg 3 (delabBody stId)))
435-    | GE.ge _ _ _ _ =>
436-      `($(← withNaryArg 2 (delabBody stId)) ≥ $(← withNaryArg 3 (delabBody stId)))
437-    | GT.gt _ _ _ _ =>
438-      `($(← withNaryArg 2 (delabBody stId)) > $(← withNaryArg 3 (delabBody stId)))
439-    | And _ _ =>
440-      `($(← withNaryArg 0 (delabBody stId)) ∧ $(← withNaryArg 1 (delabBody stId)))
441-    | Or _ _ =>
442-      `($(← withNaryArg 0 (delabBody stId)) ∨ $(← withNaryArg 1 (delabBody stId)))
443-    | Iff _ _ =>
444-      `($(← withNaryArg 0 (delabBody stId)) ↔ $(← withNaryArg 1 (delabBody stId)))
445-    | Not _ =>
446-      `(¬ $(← withAppArg (delabBody stId)))
447-    | _ =>
448-      if e.isArrow then
449-        `($(← withBindingDomain (delabBody stId)) →
450-          $(← withBindingBody `h (delabBody stId)))
451-      else if let .app f v := e then
452-        -- an applied assertion `P st` (or an applied escape lambda)
453-        guard (v == .fvar stId)
454-        guard !(f.containsFVar stId)
455-        withAppFn delab
456-      else
457-        failure
458-
459-/-- Print an `Assertion`-valued term as it appears inside `{{ … }}`: a
460-state lambda is un-threaded; a term the printer cannot rebuild falls back
461-to the raw lambda, which is exactly this notation's escape form. -/
462-partial def delabAssn : DelabM Term := do
463-  if (← getExpr).isLambda then
464-    (withBindingBody' `st (pure ·.fvarId!) fun stId => delabBody stId)
465-      <|> Delaborator.delab
466-  else
467-    delab
468-
469-/-- Print an assertion-position argument: a state lambda gets the
470-`{{ … }}` notation; any other term (a named assertion, a substitution)
471-already reads well bare. -/
472-def delabAssnArg (i : Nat) : DelabM Term := do
473-  if (← withNaryArg i getExpr).isLambda then
474-    `({{ $(← withNaryArg i delabAssn) }})
475-  else
476-    withNaryArg i Delaborator.delab
477-
478-/-- Print a bare assertion lambda in `{{ … }}` notation.  Keyed on lambdas
479-at large, so the guards bail out cheaply unless the binder is a `State`
480-and the body is a proposition the printer can rebuild. -/
481-@[delab lam]
482-def delabAssertion : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
483-  let e ← getExpr
484-  guard <| e.isLambda && e.bindingDomain!.isConstOf ``_root_.State
485-  let P ← withBindingBody' `st (pure ·.fvarId!) fun stId => do
486-    guard (← Meta.inferType (← getExpr)).isProp
487-    delabBody stId
488-  `({{ $P }})
489-
490-end Assertion.Delab
491-
492--- END DETAILS

494--- ### Assertion Implication
495-
496--- Given two assertions `P` and `Q`, we say that `P` *implies*
497--- `Q`, written `P ->> Q`, if, whenever `P` holds in some state
498--- `st`, `Q` also holds.
499-
500-def AssertImplies (P Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
501-  ∀ st, P st → Q st
502-
503--- Note that the notation for *assertion implication* is
504--- analogous to the "usual" Lean implication `→`.
505-
506-notation:26 P:27 " ->> " Q:27 => AssertImplies P Q
507-
508-theorem assertImplies_def {P Q : Assertion} : P ->> Q ↔ ∀ st, P st → Q st := by rfl
509-
510--- We'll also want the "iff" variant of implication between
511--- assertions:
512-
513-notation:26 P:27 " <<->> " Q:27 => AssertImplies P Q ∧ AssertImplies Q P
514-
515-theorem assertIff_def {P Q : Assertion} : P <<->> Q ↔ AssertImplies P Q ∧ AssertImplies Q P
516-    := by rfl
517-
518--- THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: printing implications back
519-
520-namespace Assertion.Delab
521-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr
522-
523-@[delab app.AssertImplies]
524-def delabAssertImplies : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
525-  guard <| (← getExpr).isAppOfArity ``AssertImplies 2
526-  `($(← delabAssnArg 0) ->> $(← delabAssnArg 1))
527-
528-/-- `<<->>` abbreviates a conjunction of two `AssertImplies`, so its
529-delaborator is keyed on `∧` and bails out unless the two conjuncts mirror
530-each other. -/
531-@[delab app.And]
532-def delabAssertIff : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
533-  let e ← getExpr
534-  guard <| e.isAppOfArity ``And 2
535-  let l := e.appFn!.appArg!
536-  let r := e.appArg!
537-  guard <| l.isAppOfArity ``AssertImplies 2 && r.isAppOfArity ``AssertImplies 2
538-  guard <| l.appFn!.appArg! == r.appArg! && l.appArg! == r.appFn!.appArg!
539-  `($(← withNaryArg 0 <| delabAssnArg 0) <<->> $(← withNaryArg 0 <| delabAssnArg 1))
540-
541-end Assertion.Delab
542-

545--- ## Hoare Triples, Informally
546-
547--- A *Hoare triple* is a claim about the state before and after
548--- executing a command. A commond notation for Hoare triples,
549--- and the one we use in this book, is
550-
551---   {{P}} c {{Q}}
552-
553--- meaning:
554-
555--- - If command `c` begins execution in a state satisfying
556---   assertion `P`,
557-
558--- - and if `c` eventually terminates in some final state,
559-
560--- - then that final state will satisfy the assertion `Q`.
561-
562--- Assertion `P` is called the *precondition* of the triple,
563--- and `Q` is the *postcondition*.
564-
565--- For example,
566-
567--- - The Hoare triple
568-
569---   {{X = 0}} X := X + 1 {{X = 1}}
570-
571--- states that command `X := X + 1` will transform a state in
572--- which `X = 0` to a state in which `X = 1`.
573-
574--- - On the other hand,
575-
576---   ∀ m, {{X = m}} X := X + 1 {{X = m + 1}}
577-
578--- is a *proposition* stating that the Hoare triple
579--- `{{X = m}} X :=
580--- X + 1 {{X = m + 1}}` is valid for any choice
581--- of `m`. Note that `m` in the two assertions is a reference
582--- to the *Lean* variable `m`, which is bound outside the Hoare
583--- triple.
584-
585--- _Quiz:_
586-
587--- Paraphrase the following in English.
588-
589---   1) {{True}} c {{X = 5}}
590-
591---   2) ∀ m, {{X = m}} c {{X = m + 5}}
592-
593---   3) {{X ≤ Y}} c {{Y ≤ X}}
594-
595---   4) {{True}} c {{False}}
596-
597---   5) ∀ m,
598---        {{X = m}}
599---        c
600---        {{Y = real_fact m}}
601-
602---   6) ∀ m,
603---        {{X = m}}
604---        c
605---        {{(Z * Z) ≤ m ∧ ¬ ((Z + 1) * (Z + 1) ≤ m)}}
606-
607--- _Quiz:_
608-
609--- Is the following Hoare triple *valid* -- i.e., is the
610--- claimed relation between `P`, `c`, and `Q` true?
611-
612---   {{True}} X := 5 {{X = 5}}
613-
614--- (A) Yes
615-
616--- (B) No
617-
618--- _Quiz:_
619-
620--- What about this one?
621-
622---   {{X = 2}} X := X + 1 {{X = 3}}
623-
624--- (A) Yes
625-
626--- (B) No
627-
628--- _Quiz:_
629-
630--- What about this one?
631-
632---   {{True}} X := 5; Y := 0 {{X = 5}}
633-
634--- (A) Yes
635-
636--- (B) No
637-
638--- _Quiz:_
639-
640--- What about this one?
641-
642---   {{X = 2 ∧ X = 3}} X := 5 {{X = 0}}
643-
644--- (A) Yes
645-
646--- (B) No
647-
648--- _Quiz:_
649-
650--- What about this one?
651-
652---   {{True}} skip {{False}}
653-
654--- (A) Yes
655-
656--- (B) No
657-
658--- _Quiz:_
659-
660--- What about this one?
661-
662---   {{False}} skip {{True}}
663-
664--- (A) Yes
665-
666--- (B) No
667-
668--- _Quiz:_
669-
670--- What about this one?
671-
672---   {{True}} while true do skip end {{False}}
673-
674--- (A) Yes
675-
676--- (B) No
677-

679-
680--- This one?
681-
682---   {{X = 0}}
683---     while X = 0 do X := X + 1 end
684---   {{X = 1}}
685-
686--- (A) Yes

696---   {{X = 100}}

702--- ## Hoare Triples, Formally
703-
704--- We formalize valid Hoare triples in Lean as follows:
705-
706-open scoped HasEval
707-
708-def ValidHoareTriple
709-    (P : Assertion) (c : Com) (Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
710-  ∀ {st st' : State},
711-    (st =[ c ]=> st') →
712-    P st →
713-    Q st'
714-
715--- Note to developers (Niklas Halonen @xhalo32):
716---     Somethings strange is going on in `theorem if_example`,
717---     using `apply hoare_consequence_pre` followed by
718---     `· exact hoare_asgn` works, but
719---     `refine hoare_consequence_pre hoare_asgn ?_` or
720---     `apply hoare_consequence_pre hoare_asgn` don't. The only
721---     solution I found was to mark `ValidHoareTriple`
722---     irreducible.
723---
724---     It has to do something with `apply` and `refine` looking
725---     inside the implication in `∀ {st st'}, ...`
726-
727--- Notation for Hoare triples. The command between the two
728--- assertions is parsed with the same grammar as the
729--- `imp { … }` notation, so a command that is a Lean variable
730--- (rather than concrete syntax) is spliced in with `~c`, just
731--- as in the `st =[ c ]=> st'` notation.
732-
733-class HasTriple (Com : Type) where
734-  Triple : Assertion → Com → Assertion → Prop
735-
736-namespace HasTriple
737-
738-/-- Hoare triple: `{{ P }} c {{ Q }}` -/
739-scoped notation:lead "{{" P "}} " c:lead " {{" Q "}}" => Triple ({{ P }}) c ({{ Q }})
740-
741-/-- Hoare triple with `imp_com` command syntax -/
742-scoped syntax:lead (priority := high) "{{" term "}} " imp_com:lead " {{" term "}}" : term
743-scoped macro_rules
744-  | `({{ $P }} $c:imp_com {{ $Q }}) =>
745-      ``(HasTriple.Triple ({{ $P }}) (imp { $c }) ({{ $Q }}))
746-end HasTriple
747-
748-instance : HasTriple Com where
749-  Triple := ValidHoareTriple
750-
751-open scoped HasTriple
752-
753-theorem validHoareTriple_def {P : Assertion} {c : Com} {Q : Assertion} :
754-    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} ↔ ∀ {st st' : State},
755-      (st =[ c ]=> st') →
756-      P st →
757-      Q st' := by rfl
758-
759-attribute [irreducible] ValidHoareTriple
760-
761--- THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: printing triples back
762-
763--- The delaborator is agnostic to the command type: it prints
764--- the command with whatever printer is registered for its
765--- constructors and splices the result into the triple, so a
766--- language-extension chapter only has to register a printer
767--- for its own `Com`.
768-
769-namespace Assertion.Delab
770-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr Imp.Delab
771-@[delab app.HasTriple.Triple]
772-def delabTriple : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
773-  guard <| (← getExpr).isAppOfArity ``HasTriple.Triple 5
774-  let P ← withNaryArg 2 delabAssn
775-  let c ← withNaryArg 3 delab
776-  let Q ← withNaryArg 4 delabAssn
777-  match c with
778-  | `(imp { $c:imp_com }) => ``({{ $P }} $c:imp_com {{ $Q }})
779-  | c => ``({{ $P }} ~$c {{ $Q }})
780-
781-end Assertion.Delab
782-
783--- END DETAILS

806--- ## Proof Rules
807-
808--- We want to be able to *prove* Hoare triples formally.
809-
810--- Here's our plan:
811-
812--- - introduce one "proof rule" for each Imp syntactic form
813-
814--- - plus a couple of "structural rules" that help glue proofs
815---   together
816-
817--- - prove these rules correct in terms of the definition of
818---   `ValidHoareTriple`
819-
820--- - prove programs correct using these proof rules, without ever
821---   unfolding the definition of `ValidHoareTriple`
822-
823--- ### Skip
824-
825--- Since `skip` doesn't change the state, it preserves any
826--- assertion `P`:
827-
828---   --------------------  (hoare_skip)
829---   {{ P }} skip {{ P }}
830-
831-theorem hoare_skip {P : Assertion} :
832-    {{ P }} skip {{ P }} := by
833-  rw [validHoareTriple_def]
834-  intro st st' h hpre
835-  inversion h
836-  exact hpre
837-
838--- ### Sequencing
839-
840--- If command `c1` takes any state where `P` holds to a state
841--- where `Q` holds, and if `c2` takes any state where `Q` holds
842--- to one where `R` holds, then doing `c1` followed by `c2`
843--- will take any state where `P` holds to one where `R` holds:
844-
845---    {{ P }} c1 {{ Q }}
846---    {{ Q }} c2 {{ R }}
847---   ----------------------  (hoare_seq)
848---   {{ P }} c1; c2 {{ R }}
849-
850-theorem hoare_seq {P Q R : Assertion} {c1 c2 : Com}
851-    (h1 : {{ Q }} ~c2 {{ R }}) (h2 : {{ P }} ~c1 {{ Q }}) :
852-    {{ P }} ~c1; ~c2 {{ R }} := by
853-  rw [validHoareTriple_def]
854-  intro st st' h hpre
855-  inversion h with
856-  | seq st'' hc1 hc2 =>
857-    rw [validHoareTriple_def] at h1 h2
858-    exact h1 hc2 (h2 hc1 hpre)
859-
860--- ### Assignment
861-
862--- How can we complete this triple?
863-
864---   {{ ??? }}  X := Y  {{ X = 1 }}
865-
866--- One natural possibility is:
867-
868---   {{ Y = 1 }}  X := Y  {{ X = 1 }}
869-
870--- The precondition is just the postcondition, but with `X`
871--- replaced by `Y`.
872-
873--- How about this one?
874-
875---   {{ ??? }}  X := X + Y  {{ X = 1 }}
876-
877--- Replace `X` with `X + Y`:
878-
879---   {{ X + Y = 1 }}  X := X + Y  {{ X = 1 }}
880-
881--- This works because "equals 1" holding of `X` is guaranteed
882--- by the property "equals 1" holding of whatever is being
883--- assigned to `X`.
884-
885--- In general, the postcondition could be some arbitrary
886--- assertion `Q`, and the right-hand side of the assignment
887--- could be some arbitrary arithmetic expression `a`:
888-
889---   {{ ??? }}  X := a  {{ Q }}
890-
891--- The precondition would then be `Q`, but with any occurrences
892--- of `X` in it replaced by `a`.
893-
894--- Let's introduce a notation for this idea of replacing
895--- occurrences: Define `Q \[X ↦ a`] to mean "`Q` where `a` is
896--- substituted in place of `X`".
897-
898--- This yields the Hoare logic rule for assignment:
899-
900---   {{ Q [X ↦ a] }}  X := a  {{ Q }}
901-
902--- One way of reading this rule is: If you want statement
903--- `X := a` to terminate in a state that satisfies assertion
904--- `Q`, then it suffices to start in a state that also
905--- satisfies `Q`, except where `a` is substituted for every
906--- occurrence of `X`.
907-
908--- Here are some valid instances of the assignment rule:
909-
910---   {{ (X ≤ 5) [X ↦ X + 1] }}         (that is, X + 1 ≤ 5)
911---     X := X + 1
912---   {{ X ≤ 5 }}
913-
914---   {{ (X = 3) [X ↦ 3] }}              (that is, 3 = 3)
915---     X := 3
916---   {{ X = 3 }}
917-
918---   {{ (0 ≤ X ∧ X ≤ 5) [X ↦ 3] }}.  (that is, 0 ≤ 3 ∧ 3 ≤ 5)
919---     X := 3
920---   {{ 0 ≤ X ∧ X ≤ 5 }}
921-
922--- To formalize the rule, we must first formalize the idea of
923--- "substituting an expression for an Imp variable in an
924--- assertion", which we refer to as assertion substitution, or
925--- `Assertion.subst`.
926-
927--- Intuitively, given a proposition `P`, a variable `X`, and an
928--- arithmetic expression `a`, we want to derive another
929--- proposition `P'` that is just the same as `P` except that
930--- `P'` should mention `a` wherever `P` mentions `X`.
931-
932--- This operation is related to the idea of substituting Imp

1003--- That is, `P [X ↦ a]` stands for an assertion -- let's call
1004--- it `P'` -- that behaves just like `P` except that, wherever
1005--- `P` looks up the variable `X` in the current state, `P'`
1006--- instead uses the value of the expression `a`.

1010--- logical equivalences:

1016-  rw [assertImplies_def]

1018-  · intro st _
1019-    simp
1020-  · intro st h
1021-    simp

1026-  constructor
1027-  · rw [assertImplies_def]
1028-    intro st
1029-    simp

1040--- Now, using the substitution operation we've just defined, we
1041--- can give the precise proof rule for assignment:
1042-
1043---   ---------------------------- (hoare_asgn)
1044---   {{Q [X ↦ a]}} X := a {{Q}}
1045-
1046--- We can prove formally that this rule is indeed valid.
1047-
1048-theorem hoare_asgn {Q : Assertion} {x : Ident} {a : Aexp} :
1049-    {{ Q [x ↦ ~a] }} x := ~a {{ Q }} := by
1050-  rw [validHoareTriple_def]
1051-  intro st st' hE hQ
1052-  inversion hE with
1053-  | asgn n h =>
1054-    subst h
1055-    rw [Assertion.subst_def] at hQ
1056-    exact hQ

1059--- rule.

1062-    {{ (X < 5) [X ↦ X + 1] }}
1063-      X := X + 1
1064-    {{ X < 5 }} := by
1065-  exact hoare_asgn

1080--- ### Consequence
1081-
1082--- Sometimes the preconditions and postconditions we get from
1083--- the Hoare rules won't quite be the ones we want in the
1084--- particular situation at hand -- they may be logically
1085--- equivalent but have a different syntactic form that fails to
1086--- unify with the goal we are trying to prove, or they actually
1087--- may be logically weaker (for preconditions) or stronger (for
1088--- postconditions) than what we need.
1089-
1090--- For instance,
1091-
1092---   {{(X = 3) [X ↦ 3]}} X := 3 {{X = 3}},
1093-
1094--- follows directly from the assignment rule, but
1095-
1096---   {{True}} X := 3 {{X = 3}}
1097-
1098--- does not. This triple is valid, but it is not an instance of
1099--- `hoare_asgn` because `True` and `(X = 3) \[X ↦ 3`] are not
1100--- syntactically equal assertions.
1101-
1102--- However, they are logically *equivalent*, so if one triple
1103--- is valid, then the other must certainly be as well. We can
1104--- capture this observation with the following rule:
1105-
1106---      {{P'}} c {{Q}}
1107---        P <<->> P'
1108---   ---------------------
1109---      {{P}} c {{Q}}
1110-
1111--- Taking this line of thought a bit further, we can see that
1112--- strengthening the precondition or weakening the
1113--- postcondition of a valid triple always produces another
1114--- valid triple. This observation is captured by two *Rules of
1115--- Consequence*.
1116-
1117---          {{P'}} c {{Q}}
1118---             P ->> P'
1119---   -----------------------------   (hoare_consequence_pre)
1120---          {{P}} c {{Q}}
1121-
1122---          {{P}} c {{Q'}}
1123---            Q' ->> Q
1124---   -----------------------------    (hoare_consequence_post)
1125---          {{P}} c {{Q}}
1126-
1127--- Here are the formal versions:
1128-
1129-theorem hoare_consequence_pre {P P' Q : Assertion} {c : Com}
1130-    (hhoare : {{ P' }} ~c {{ Q }}) (himp : P ->> P') :
1131-    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
1132-  rw [validHoareTriple_def] at hhoare ⊢
1133-  intro st st' heval hpre
1134-  apply hhoare heval
1135-  rw [assertImplies_def] at himp
1136-  exact himp _ hpre
1137-
1138-theorem hoare_consequence_post {P Q Q' : Assertion} {c : Com}
1139-    (hhoare : {{ P }} ~c {{ Q' }}) (himp : Q' ->> Q) :
1140-    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
1141-  rw [validHoareTriple_def] at hhoare ⊢
1142-  intro st st' heval hpre
1143-  rw [assertImplies_def] at himp
1144-  apply himp
1145-  exact hhoare heval hpre
1146-
1147--- For example, we can use the first consequence rule like
1148--- this:
1149-
1150---   {{ True }} ->>
1151---   {{ (X = 1) [X ↦ 1] }}
1152---     X := 1
1153---   {{ X = 1 }}
1154-
1155--- Or, formally...
1156-
1157-theorem hoare_asgn_example1 :
1158-    {{True}} X := 1 {{X = 1}} := by
1159-  sorry
1160-
1161--- We can also use it to prove the example mentioned earlier.
1162-
1163---   {{ X < 4 }} ->>
1164---   {{ (X < 5)[X ↦ X + 1] }}
1165---     X := X + 1
1166---   {{ X < 5 }}
1167-
1168--- Or, formally ...

1173-    {{X < 5}} := by

1177---     The above proof uses `simp_all` purely because `lia`

1181--- Finally, here is a combined rule of consequence that allows
1182--- us to vary both the precondition and the postcondition.
1183-
1184---          {{P'}} c {{Q'}}
1185---             P ->> P'
1186---             Q' ->> Q
1187---   -----------------------------   (hoare_consequence)
1188---          {{P}} c {{Q}}

1191---     In the following proof, `(P' := P')` is not necessary,
1192---     however it avoids having a metavariable in the first
1193---     goal. Another option is to just write
1194---     `exact hoare_consequence_pre (hoare_consequence_post htriple hpost) hpre`.
1195-
1196-theorem hoare_consequence {P P' Q Q' : Assertion} {c : Com}
1197-    (htriple : {{ P' }} ~c {{ Q' }}) (hpre : P ->> P') (hpost : Q' ->> Q) :
1198-    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
1199-  apply hoare_consequence_pre (P' := P')
1200-  · exact hoare_consequence_post htriple hpost
1201-  · exact hpre

1203--- ### Automation
1204-
1205--- Many of the proofs we have done so far with Hoare triples
1206--- can be streamlined using the automation techniques that we
1207--- introduced in the *Automation* chapter of *Logical
1208--- Foundations*.
1209-
1210--- Recall that `simp` rewrites with any lemmas we pass it. The
1211--- definitions whose meaning we keep needing to expose in this
1212--- chapter -- `ValidHoareTriple`, `AssertImplies`, and
1213--- `Assertion.subst` -- each come with a characterizing lemma
1214--- (`validHoareTriple_def`, `assertImplies_def`,
1215--- `Assertion.subst_def`) restating the definition as an
1216--- equation. Passing these lemmas to `simp` replaces the
1217--- defined notions by their meanings wherever they appear.
1218--- We'll do that explicitly below (and shortly package the
1219--- recipe up as a tactic of our own).
1220-

1222---     The Rocq source here registers
1223---     `Hint Unfold assert_implies assertion_sub
1224---     t_update : core`
1225---     for `auto`. That only widens `auto`'s search (unlike the
1226---     `Arguments /.` commands, it does not affect `simpl`), so
1227---     its Lean counterpart is the `assertion_auto` tactic's
1228---     simp list below -- not global `@[simp]` lemmas as for
1229---     the notation wrappers, whose folded names carry no
1230---     meaning in goals the way `->>` and `Assertion.subst` do.

1367-
1368--- Here's an example of a program involving both sequencing and
1369--- assignment. Note the use of `hoare_seq` in conjunction with
1370--- `hoare_consequence_pre` and `apply`'s metavariables.
1371-
1372-theorem hoare_asgn_example3 (a : Aexp) (n : Nat) :
1373-    {{a = n}}
1374-      X := ~a;
1375-      skip
1376-    {{X = n}} := by
1377-  apply hoare_seq
1378-  · -- right part of seq
1379-    exact hoare_skip
1380-  · -- left part of seq
1381-    apply hoare_consequence_pre
1382-    · exact hoare_asgn
1383-    · assertion_auto

1385--- Informally, a nice way of displaying a proof using the
1386--- sequencing rule is as a "decorated program" where the
1387--- intermediate assertion `Q` is written between `c1` and `c2`:
1388-
1389---            {{ a = n }}
1390---   X := a
1391---            {{ X = n }};    <--- decoration for Q
1392---   skip
1393---            {{ X = n }}

1398--- ### Conditionals
1399-
1400--- What sort of rule do we want for reasoning about conditional
1401--- commands?
1402-
1403--- Certainly, if the same assertion `Q` holds after executing
1404--- either of the branches, then it holds after the whole
1405--- conditional. So we might be tempted to write:
1406-
1407---           {{P}} c1 {{Q}}
1408---           {{P}} c2 {{Q}}
1409---   ---------------------------------
1410---   {{P}} if b then c1 else c2 {{Q}}
1411-
1412--- However, this is rather weak. For example, using this rule,
1413--- we cannot show
1414-
1415---   {{ True }}
1416---     if X = 0
1417---       then Y := 2
1418---       else Y := X + 1
1419---     end
1420---   {{ X ≤ Y }}
1421-
1422--- since the rule doesn't tell us enough about the state in
1423--- which the assignments take place in the "then" and "else"
1424--- branches.
1425-
1426--- Better:
1427-
1428---   {{P ∧   b}} c1 {{Q}}
1429---   {{P ∧ ¬ b}} c2 {{Q}}
1430---   ------------------------------------  (hoare_if)
1431---   {{P}} if b then c1 else c2 end {{Q}}
1432-

1434---     I have removed `bassertion` as it's an unnecessary
1435---     abstraction and only adds overhead for the reader.

1440-    ¬ ({{ b }}) st := by
1441-  dsimp

1449--- Now we can formalize the Hoare proof rule for conditionals
1450--- and prove it correct.
1451-
1452--- The statement of the rule reads: given
1453--- `htrue : {{ P ∧ b }} ~c1 {{Q}}` and
1454--- `hfalse : {{ P ∧ ¬b }} ~c2 {{Q}}`, we can conclude
1455--- `{{P}} if (~b) { ~c1 } else { ~c2 } {{Q}}`.
1456-
1457-theorem hoare_if {P Q : Assertion} {b : Bexp} {c1 c2 : Com}
1458-    (htrue : {{ P ∧ b }} ~c1 {{ Q }}) (hfalse : {{ P ∧ ¬ b }} ~c2 {{ Q }}) :
1459-    {{ P }} if (~b) { ~c1 } else { ~c2 } {{ Q }} := by
1460-  rw [validHoareTriple_def] at htrue hfalse ⊢
1461-  intro st st' hE hpre
1462-  inversion hE with
1463-  | ifTrue hb hc1 =>
1464-    exact htrue hc1 ⟨hpre, hb⟩
1465-  | ifFalse hb hc =>
1466-    rw [← Bool.not_eq_true] at hb
1467-    exact hfalse hc ⟨hpre, hb⟩

1505--- ### While Loops
1506-
1507--- The Hoare rule for `while` loops is based on the idea of a
1508--- *command invariant* (or just *invariant*): an assertion
1509--- whose truth is guaranteed after executing a command,
1510--- assuming it is true before.
1511-
1512--- That is, an assertion `P` is a command invariant of `c` if
1513-
1514---   {{P}} c {{P}}
1515-
1516--- holds. Note that the command invariant might temporarily
1517--- become false in the middle of executing `c`, but by the end
1518--- of `c` it must be restored.
1519-
1520--- The Hoare while rule combines the idea of a command
1521--- invariant with information about when guard `b` does or does
1522--- not hold.
1523-
1524---         {{P ∧ b}} c {{P}}
1525---   --------------------------------- (hoare_while)
1526---   {{P}} while b do c end {{P ∧ ¬b}}
1527-

1530---     guess it's folded...

1535-theorem hoare_while {P : Assertion} {b : Bexp} {c : Com}
1536-    (hhoare : {{P ∧ b}} ~c {{ P }}) :
1537-    {{ P }} while (~b) { ~c } {{P ∧ ¬ b}} := by
1538-  rw [validHoareTriple_def] at hhoare ⊢
1539-  intro st st' heval hpre
1540-  /- We proceed by induction on `heval`, because, in the "keep
1541-  looping" case, its hypotheses talk about the whole loop instead
1542-  of just `c`. We begin by generalizing over an
1543-  arbitrary command, together with an equation remembering that the
1544-  command is the original loop. The cases for commands other than
1545-  `while` are dismissed because their equations are contradictory. -/
1546-  generalize heq : (imp { while (~b) { ~c } }) = cmd at heval
1547-  induction heval with
1548-  | @whileFalse b0 s0 c0 hb =>
1549-    injection heq with hbeq hceq
1550-    simp_all
1551-  | @whileTrue s0 s0' s0'' b0 c0 hb hc hloop ih1 ih2 =>
1552-    injection heq with hbeq hceq
1553-    subst hbeq hceq
1554-    exact ih2 (hhoare hc ⟨hpre, hb⟩) rfl
1555-  | skip | asgn | seq | ifTrue | ifFalse =>
1556-    contradiction

1575--- We call `P` a *loop invariant* of `while b do c end` if
1576-
1577---   {{P ∧ b}} c {{P}}
1578-
1579--- is a valid Hoare triple.
1580-
1581--- This means that `P` will be true at the end of the loop body
1582--- whenever the loop body executes. If `P` contradicts `b`,
1583--- this holds trivially since the precondition is false.
1584-
1585--- For instance, `X = 0` is a loop invariant of
1586-
1587---   while X = 2 do X := 1 end
1588-
1589--- since the program will never enter the loop.

1723--- ## Summary
1724-
1725--- The rules of Hoare Logic are:
1726-
1727---          --------------------------- (hoare_asgn)
1728---          {{Q [X ↦ a]}} X:=a {{Q}}
1729-
1730---          --------------------  (hoare_skip)
1731---          {{ P }} skip {{ P }}
1732-
1733---            {{ P }} c1 {{ Q }}
1734---            {{ Q }} c2 {{ R }}
1735---           ----------------------  (hoare_seq)
1736---           {{ P }} c1;c2 {{ R }}
1737-
1738---           {{P ∧   b}} c1 {{Q}}
1739---           {{P ∧ ¬ b}} c2 {{Q}}
1740---   ------------------------------------  (hoare_if)
1741---   {{P}} if b then c1 else c2 end {{Q}}
1742-
1743---            {{P ∧ b}} c {{P}}
1744---     -----------------------------------  (hoare_while)
1745---     {{P}} while b do c end {{P ∧ ¬ b}}
1746-
1747---             {{P'}} c {{Q'}}
1748---                P ->> P'
1749---                Q' ->> Q
1750---      -----------------------------   (hoare_consequence)
1751---             {{P}} c {{Q}}
1752-
1753--- Our main task in this chapter has been to *define* the rules
1754--- of Hoare logic, and prove that the definitions are sound.
1755--- Having done so, we can go on and work *within* Hoare logic
1756--- to prove that particular programs satisfy particular Hoare
1757--- triples. In the next chapter, we'll see how Hoare logic is
1758--- can be used to prove that more interesting programs satisfy
1759--- interesting specifications of their behavior.
1760-
1761--- Crucially, we will do so without ever again `unfold`ing the
1762--- definition of Hoare triples -- i.e., we will take the rules
1763--- of Hoare logic as a closed world for reasoning about
1764--- programs.
1765-

124--- ## Decorated Programs
125-
126--- The beauty of Hoare Logic is that it is *syntax directed*:
127--- the structure of proofs exactly follows the structure of
128--- programs.
129-
130--- We can record the essential ideas of a Hoare-logic proof —
131--- omitting low-level calculational details — by "decorating" a
132--- program with appropriate assertions on each of its commands.
133-
134--- Such a *decorated program* carries within itself an argument
135--- for its own correctness.
136-
137--- For example, consider the program:
138-
139---   X := m;
140---   Z := p;
141---   while X <> 0 do
142---     Z := Z - 1;
143---     X := X - 1
144---   end
145-
146--- Here is one possible specification for this program, in the
147--- form of a Hoare triple:
148-
149---   {{ True }}
150---   X := m;
151---   Z := p;
152---   while X <> 0 do
153---     Z := Z - 1;
154---     X := X - 1
155---   end
156---   {{ Z = p - m }}
157-
158--- Here is a decorated version of this program, embodying a
159--- proof of this specification:
160-
161---   {{ True }} ->>
162---   {{ m = m }}
163---     X := m
164---                        {{ X = m }} ->>
165---                        {{ X = m /\ p = p }};
166---     Z := p;
167---                        {{ X = m /\ Z = p }} ->>
168---                        {{ Z - X = p - m }}
169---     while X <> 0 do
170---                        {{ Z - X = p - m /\ X <> 0 }} ->>
171---                        {{ (Z - 1) - (X - 1) = p - m }}
172---       Z := Z - 1
173---                        {{ Z - (X - 1) = p - m }};
174---       X := X - 1
175---                        {{ Z - X = p - m }}
176---     end
177---   {{ Z - X = p - m /\ ~ (X <> 0) }} ->>
178---   {{ Z = p - m }}

202-
203--- Concretely, a decorated program consists of the program's
204--- text interleaved with assertions (sometimes multiple
205--- assertions separated by ->>).
206-
207--- A decorated program can be viewed as a compact
208--- representation of a proof in Hoare Logic: the assertions
209--- surrounding each command specify the Hoare triple to be
210--- proved for that part of the program using one of the Hoare
211--- Logic rules, and the structure of the program itself shows
212--- how to assemble all these individual steps into a proof for
213--- the whole program.
214-
215--- ### Example: Swapping
216-
217--- Consider the following program, which swaps the values of
218--- two variables using addition and subtraction, instead of by
219--- assigning to a temporary variable.
220-
221---   X := X + Y;
222---   Y := X - Y;
223---   X := X - Y
224-
225--- We can give a proof, in the form of decorations, that this
226--- program is correct — i.e., it really swaps `X` and `Y` — as
227--- follows.

279--- ### Example: Division
280-
281--- Let's do one more example of simple reasoning about a loop.
282-
283--- The following Imp program calculates the integer quotient
284--- and remainder of parameters `m` and `n`.
285-
286---   X := m;
287---   Y := 0;
288---   while n <= X do
289---     X := X - n;
290---     Y := Y + 1
291---   end;
292-
293--- If we replace `m` and `n` by concrete numbers and execute
294--- the program, it will terminate with the variable `X` set to
295--- the remainder when `m` is divided by `n` and `Y` set to the
296--- quotient.
297-
298--- Here's a possible specification:
299-
300---   {{ True }}
301---     X := m;
302---     Y := 0;
303---     while n <= X do
304---       X := X - n;
305---       Y := Y + 1
306---     end
307---   {{ n * Y + X = m /\ X < n }}
308-

311--- ### From Decorated Programs to Formal Proofs
312-
313--- From an informal proof in the form of a decorated program,
314--- it is "easy in principle" to read off a formal proof using
315--- the Lean theorems corresponding to the Hoare Logic rules,
316--- but these proofs can be a bit long and fiddly.
317-
318--- For example...
319-
320-def reduceToZero : Com :=
321-  imp {
322-    while (X ≠ 0) {
323-      X := X - 1
324-    }
325-  }
326-
327-theorem reduce_to_zero_correct' :
328-    {{ True }} ~reduceToZero {{ X = 0 }} := by
329-  -- First put the postcondition into the form expected by
330-  -- the while rule.
331-  sorry

334--- helping deal with the boring parts of the process of proving
335--- assertions:
336-

338-  `(tactic| assertion_auto)

346--- This example shows that it is conceptually straightforward
347--- to read off the main elements of a formal proof from a
348--- decorated program. Indeed, the process is so straightforward
349--- that it can be automated, as we will see next.
350-
351--- ## Formal Decorated Programs
352-
353--- With a little more work, we can *formalize* the definition
354--- of well-formed decorated programs and *automate* the boring
355--- mechanical steps in proving that the decorations are
356--- correct.
357-
358--- ### Syntax
359-
360--- The first thing we need to do is to formalize a variant of
361--- the syntax of Imp commands that includes embedded
362--- assertions, which we'll call "decorations." We call the new
363--- commands *decorated commands*, or `dcom`s.
364-
365--- The choice of exactly where to put assertions in the
366--- definition of `dcom` is a bit subtle. The simplest thing to
367--- do would be to annotate every `dcom` with a precondition and
368--- postcondition — something like this...
369-
370-namespace DComFirstTry
371-
372-inductive DCom where
373-  | skip (pre : Assertion)
374-  | seq (pre : Assertion) (first : DCom)
375-      (middle : Assertion)
376-      (second : DCom) (post : Assertion)
377-  | asgn (x : Ident) (a : Aexp) (post : Assertion)
378-  | cond (pre : Assertion) (b : Bexp)
379-      (thenPre : Assertion) (thenBranch : DCom)
380-      (elsePre : Assertion) (elseBranch : DCom)
381-      (post : Assertion)
382-  | whileDo (pre : Assertion) (b : Bexp)
383-      (bodyPre : Assertion) (body : DCom)
384-      (bodyPost : Assertion) (post : Assertion)
385-  | strengthenPre (pre : Assertion) (body : DCom)
386-  | weakenPost (body : DCom) (post : Assertion)
387-
388-end DComFirstTry
389-
390--- But this would result in *very* verbose decorated programs
391--- with a lot of repeated annotations: a simple program like
392--- `skip;skip` would be decorated like this,
393-
394---   {{P}} ({{P}} skip {{P}}) ; ({{P}} skip {{P}}) {{P}}
395-
396--- with pre- and post-conditions around each `skip`, plus
397--- identical pre- and post-conditions on the semicolon!
398-
399--- In other words, we don't want both preconditions and
400--- postconditions on each command, because a sequence of two
401--- commands would contain redundant decorations — the
402--- postcondition of the first likely being the same as the
403--- precondition of the second.
404-
405--- Instead, our formal syntax of decorated commands will omit
406--- preconditions whenever possible and embed just
407--- postconditions.
408-
409--- - The `skip` command, for example, is decorated only with its
410---   postcondition
411-
412---   skip {{ Q }}
413-
414--- on the assumption that the precondition will be provided by
415--- somebody else.
416-
417--- We carry the same assumption through the other syntactic
418--- forms: each decorated command is assumed to carry its own
419--- postcondition within itself but take its precondition from
420--- its context in which it is used.
421-
422--- - Sequences `d1 ; d2` need no additional decorations.
423-
424--- Why?
425-
426--- Because inside `d2` there will be a postcondition, which
427--- also serves as the postcondition of `d1;d2`.
428-
429--- Similarly, inside `d1` there will also be a postcondition,
430--- which additionally serves as the *precondition* for `d2`.
431-
432--- - An assignment `X := a` is decorated only with its
433---   postcondition:
434-
435---   X := a {{ Q }}
436-
437--- - A conditional `if b then d1 else d2` is decorated with a
438---   postcondition for the entire statement, as well as
439---   preconditions for each branch:
440-
441---   if b then {{ P1 }} d1 else {{ P2 }} d2 end {{ Q }}
442-
443--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00, before next release, 2025):
444---     Maybe we need a note here about why we don't just
445---     calculate P1 and P2 later, once we know the precondition
446---     of the whole loop. Indeed, we could (and perhaps should,
447---     as discussed elsewhere), but we are doing something
448---     simpler for the moment.
449-
450--- - A loop `while b do d end` is decorated with its final
451---   postcondition plus a precondition for the body:
452-
453---   while b do {{ P }} d end {{ Q }}
454-
455--- The postcondition embedded in `d` serves as the loop
456--- invariant.
457-
458--- - Implications `->>` can be added as decorations either for a
459---   precondition...
460-
461---   ->> {{ P }} d
462-
463--- ...or for a postcondition:
464-
465---   d ->> {{ Q }}
466-
467--- The former is waiting for another precondition to be
468--- supplied by the context; the latter relies on the
469--- postcondition already embedded in `d`.
470-
471--- Putting this all together gives us the formal syntax of
472--- decorated commands:
473-
474-inductive DCom where
475-  | skip (post : Assertion)
476-  | seq (first second : DCom)
477-  | asgn (x : Ident) (a : Aexp) (post : Assertion)
478-  | cond (b : Bexp)
479-      (thenPre : Assertion) (thenBranch : DCom)
480-      (elsePre : Assertion) (elseBranch : DCom)
481-      (post : Assertion)
482-  | whileDo (b : Bexp) (bodyPre : Assertion) (body : DCom)
483-      (post : Assertion)
484-  | pre (pre : Assertion) (body : DCom)
485-  | post (body : DCom) (post : Assertion)
486-
487--- Lean keeps decorated-command notation in its own syntax
488--- category, `dcom`, so it can coexist with the ordinary Imp
489--- command syntax.

500-  "{{" term "}}" ppLine dcom ppLine

513-  | `(dcom { ($body:dcom) }) =>
514-      `(dcom { $body })
515-  | `(dcom { skip {{ $q }} }) =>

523-          {{ $p1 }}

525-        else
526-          {{ $p2 }}

528-        end
529-          {{ $q }}
530-      }) =>
531-      `(DCom.cond (bexp { $b })
532-        ({{ $p1 }}) (dcom { $d1 })
533-        ({{ $p2 }}) (dcom { $d2 })
534-        ({{ $q }}))
535-  | `(dcom {
536-        while ($b:imp_bexp) do
537-          {{ $p }}
538-          $body:dcom
539-        end
540-          {{ $q }}
541-      }) =>
542-      `(DCom.whileDo (bexp { $b }) ({{ $p }})
543-        (dcom { $body }) ({{ $q }}))
544-  | `(dcom { ->> {{ $p }} $body:dcom }) =>
545-      `(DCom.pre ({{ $p }}) (dcom { $body }))

551--- (We then need to redefine all our Notations to get nice
552--- concrete syntax for `dcom`.)
553-
554--- To provide the initial precondition that goes at the very
555--- top of a decorated program, we introduce a new type
556--- `decorated`:
557-
558-structure Decorated where
559-  pre : Assertion
560-  body : DCom
561-
562--- Note to developers:
563---     HIDE: Add FOLD here
564-
565-example : DCom :=
566-  .skip ({{ True }})
567-
568-example : DCom :=
569-  .whileDo (bexp {true}) ({{ True }})
570-    (.skip ({{ True }})) ({{ True }})

572--- To inspect the fully elaborated term behind this notation,
573--- put `set_option pp.all true in` before a `#check` or
574--- `#print` command.
575-
576--- The formal definitions can use either constructors directly
577--- or the decorated-command notation introduced above.

582--- An example `decorated` program that decrements `X` to `0`:
583-
584-def decWhile : Decorated where
585-  pre := ({{ True }})
586-  body := dcom {
587-    while (X ≠ 0) do
588-      {{ True ∧ ¬ X = 0 }}
589-      X := X - 1 {{ True }}
590-    end
591-      {{ True ∧ X = 0 }}
592-    ->> {{ X = 0 }}
593-  }

595--- It is easy to go from a `dcom` to a `com` by erasing all
596--- annotations.
597-
598-def DCom.erase (d : DCom) : Com :=
599-  match d with
600-  | .skip _ => .skip
601-  | .seq d1 d2 => .seq d1.erase d2.erase
602-  | .asgn x a _ => .asgn x a
603-  | .cond b _ d1 _ d2 _ => .cond b d1.erase d2.erase
604-  | .whileDo b _ body _ => .whileDo b body.erase
605-  | .pre _ body => body.erase
606-  | .post body _ => body.erase
607-
608-def Decorated.erase (dec : Decorated) : Com :=
609-  dec.body.erase
610-
611--- It is also straightforward to extract the precondition and
612--- postcondition from a decorated program.
613-
614-def Decorated.precondition (dec : Decorated) : Assertion :=
615-  dec.pre
616-
617--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00, before next release, 2025):
618---     `It would be nice to use <{ ... }> notations
619---     in this definition and the ones below...
620---          | <{ skip {{P}} }>        => P
621---          | <{ _; d2 }>             => post d2
622---          | <{ _ := _ {{Q}} }>      => Q`
623-
624-def DCom.postcondition (d : DCom) : Assertion :=
625-  match d with
626-  | .skip q => q
627-  | .seq _ d2 => d2.postcondition
628-  | .asgn _ _ q => q
629-  | .cond _ _ _ _ _ q => q
630-  | .whileDo _ _ _ q => q
631-  | .pre _ body => body.postcondition
632-  | .post _ q => q
633-
634-def Decorated.postcondition (dec : Decorated) : Assertion :=
635-  dec.body.postcondition
636-
637--- We can then express what it means for a decorated program to
638--- be correct as follows:
639-
640-def Decorated.OuterTripleValid (dec : Decorated) : Prop :=
641-  ValidHoareTriple dec.precondition dec.erase
642-    dec.postcondition
643-
644--- For example:
645-
646-example :
647-    decWhile.OuterTripleValid =
648-      {{ True }}
649-        while (X ≠ 0) {
650-          X := X - 1
651-        }
652-      {{ X = 0 }} := by
653-  rfl
654-
655--- The outer Hoare triple of a decorated program is just a
656--- `Prop`; thus, to show that it is *valid*, we need to produce
657--- a proof of this proposition.
658-
659--- We will do this by extracting "proof obligations" from the
660--- decorations sprinkled throughout the program.
661-
662--- These obligations are often called *verification
663--- conditions*, because they are the facts that must be
664--- verified to see that the decorations are locally consistent
665--- and thus constitute a proof of validity of the outer triple.
666-
667--- ### Extracting Verification Conditions
668-
669--- The function `DCom.VerificationConditions` takes a decorated
670--- command `d` together with a precondition `P` and returns a
671--- *proposition* that, if it can be proved, implies that the
672--- triple
673-
674---   {{P}} d.erase {{d.postcondition}}
675-
676--- is valid.
677-
678--- It does this by walking over `d` and generating a big
679--- conjunction that includes
680-
681--- - local consistency checks for each form of command, plus
682-
683--- - uses of `->>` to bridge the gap between the assertions found
684---   inside a decorated command and the assertions imposed by the
685---   external precondition; these uses correspond to applications
686---   of the consequence rule.
687-
688--- *Local consistency* is defined as follows...
689-
690--- - The decorated command
691-
692---   skip {{Q}}
693-
694--- is locally consistent with respect to a precondition `P` if
695--- `P ->> Q`.
696-
697--- - The sequential composition of `d1` and `d2` is locally
698---   consistent with respect to `P` if `d1` is locally consistent
699---   with respect to `P` and `d2` is locally consistent with
700---   respect to the postcondition of `d1`.
701-
702--- - An assignment
703-
704---   X := a {{Q}}
705-
706--- is locally consistent with respect to a precondition `P` if:
707-
708---   P ->> Q [X |-> a]
709-
710--- - A conditional
711-
712---   if b then {{P1}} d1 else {{P2}} d2 end {{Q}}
713-
714--- is locally consistent with respect to precondition `P` if
715-
716--- (1) `P /\ b ->> P1`
717-
718--- (2) `P /\ ~b ->> P2`
719-
720--- (3) `d1` is locally consistent with respect to `P1`
721-
722--- (4) `d2` is locally consistent with respect to `P2`
723-
724--- (5) `d1.postcondition ->> Q`
725-
726--- (6) `d2.postcondition ->> Q`
727-
728--- - A loop
729-
730---   while b do {{Q}} d end {{R}}
731-
732--- is locally consistent with respect to precondition `P` if:
733-
734--- (1) `P ->> d.postcondition`
735-
736--- (2) `d.postcondition /\ b ->> Q`
737-
738--- (3) `d.postcondition /\ ~b ->> R`
739-
740--- (4) `d` is locally consistent with respect to `Q`
741-
742--- - A command with an extra assertion at the beginning
743-
744---   ->> {{Q}} d
745-
746--- is locally consistent with respect to a precondition `P` if:
747-
748--- (1) `P ->> Q`
749-
750--- (2) `d` is locally consistent with respect to `Q`
751-
752--- - A command with an extra assertion at the end
753-
754---   d ->> {{Q}}
755-
756--- is locally consistent with respect to a precondition `P` if:
757-
758--- (1) `d` is locally consistent with respect to `P`
759-
760--- (2) `d.postcondition ->> Q`
761-
762--- With all this in mind, we can write a *verification
763--- condition generator* that takes a decorated command and
764--- reads off a proposition saying that all its decorations are
765--- locally consistent.
766-
767--- Formally, since a decorated command is "waiting for its
768--- precondition" the main VC generator takes a `dcom` plus a
769--- given precondition as arguments.
770-
771--- Note to developers:
772---     HIDE: There was some discussion in 2016 about whether
773---     the VC generator should should use equivalence or
774---     implication in a few places. I (BCP) believe Phil
775---     (Wadler) changed some instances of the former to the
776---     latter.
777---
778---     HIDE: MRC'20: a written explanation of each part of this
779---     would be quite nice. BCP 21: Agreed!! (BCP 23: But it's
780---     kind of what's just above...)
781-
782-def DCom.VerificationConditions
783-    (P : Assertion) (d : DCom) : Prop :=
784-  match d with
785-  | .skip Q =>
786-      P ->> Q
787-  | .seq d1 d2 =>
788-      d1.VerificationConditions P ∧
789-      d2.VerificationConditions d1.postcondition
790-  | .asgn x a Q =>
791-      P ->> {{ Q [x ↦ ~a] }}
792-  | .cond b P1 d1 P2 d2 Q =>
793-      ({{ P ∧ b }} ->> P1) ∧
794-      ({{ P ∧ ¬ b }} ->> P2) ∧
795-      (d1.postcondition ->> Q) ∧
796-      (d2.postcondition ->> Q) ∧
797-      d1.VerificationConditions P1 ∧
798-      d2.VerificationConditions P2
799-  | .whileDo b bodyPre body q =>
800-      -- The body's postcondition is both the loop invariant
801-      -- and the precondition for the first iteration.
802-      (P ->> body.postcondition) ∧
803-      ({{ body.postcondition ∧ b }} ->> bodyPre) ∧
804-      ({{ body.postcondition ∧ ¬ b }} ->> q) ∧
805-      body.VerificationConditions bodyPre
806-  | .pre P' body =>
807-      (P ->> P') ∧ body.VerificationConditions P'
808-  | .post body Q =>
809-      body.VerificationConditions P ∧
810-      (body.postcondition ->> Q)
811-
812--- The following key theorem states that
813--- `DCom.VerificationConditions` does its job correctly. Not
814--- surprisingly, each of the Hoare Logic rules plays a critical
815--- role at some point in the proof.
816-
817-theorem verification_correct (d : DCom) (P : Assertion)
818-    (hvc : d.VerificationConditions P) :
819-    ValidHoareTriple P d.erase d.postcondition := by
820-  sorry
821-
822--- Now that all the pieces are in place, we can define what it
823--- means to verify an entire program.
824-
825-def Decorated.VerificationConditions
826-    (dec : Decorated) : Prop :=
827-  dec.body.VerificationConditions dec.pre
828-
829--- And this brings us to the main theorem of this section:
830-
831-theorem verification_conditions_correct (dec : Decorated)
832-    (hvc : dec.VerificationConditions) :
833-    dec.OuterTripleValid := by
834-  exact verification_correct dec.body dec.pre hvc

862--- To automate the overall process of verification, we can use
863--- `verification_correct` to extract the verification
864--- conditions, use `verify_assertion` to verify them as much as
865--- it can, and finally tidy up any remaining bits by hand.
866-
867-macro "verify" : tactic =>
868-  `(tactic|
869-    (apply verification_conditions_correct;
870-     verify_assertion))

878--- ## Finding Loop Invariants
879-
880--- Once the outer pre- and postcondition are chosen, the only
881--- creative part in verifying programs using Hoare Logic is
882--- finding the right loop invariants...
883-
884--- ### Example: Slow Subtraction
885-
886--- The following program subtracts the value of `X` from the
887--- value of `Y` by repeatedly decrementing both `X` and `Y`. We
888--- want to verify its correctness with respect to the pre- and
889--- postconditions shown:
890-
891---   {{ X = m /\ Y = n }}
892---     while X <> 0 do
893---       Y := Y - 1;
894---       X := X - 1
895---     end
896---   {{ Y = n - m }}
897-
898--- To verify this program, we need to find an invariant `Inv`
899--- for the loop. As a first step we can leave `Inv` as an
900--- unknown and build a *skeleton* for the proof by applying the
901--- rules for local consistency, working from the end of the
902--- program to the beginning, as usual, and without doing any
903--- thinking at all yet.
904-
905--- This leads to the following skeleton:
906-
907---   (1)    {{ X = m /\ Y = n }}  ->>                   (a)
908---   (2)    {{ Inv }}
909---            while X <> 0 do
910---   (3)              {{ Inv /\ X <> 0 }}  ->>          (c)
911---   (4)              {{ Inv [X |-> X-1] [Y |-> Y-1] }}
912---              Y := Y - 1;
913---   (5)              {{ Inv [X |-> X-1] }}
914---              X := X - 1
915---   (6)              {{ Inv }}
916---            end
917---   (7)    {{ Inv /\ ~ (X <> 0) }}  ->>                (b)
918---   (8)    {{ Y = n - m }}
919-
920--- Examining this skeleton, we can see that any valid `Inv`
921--- will have to respect three conditions:
922-
923--- - (a) it must be *weak* enough to be implied by the loop's
924---   precondition, i.e., (1) must imply (2);
925-
926--- - (b) it must be *strong* enough to imply the program's
927---   postcondition, i.e., (7) must imply (8);
928-
929--- - (c) it must be *preserved* by a single iteration of the
930---   loop, assuming that the loop guard also evaluates to true,
931---   i.e., (3) must imply (4).
932-
933--- WORK IN CLASS (by filling in the previous template)

986--- ## Weakest Preconditions (Optional)
987-
988--- Note to developers:
989---     HIDE: BCP 21: We talked about moving this stuff to the
990---     HoareAsLogic chapter to lighten this chapter, but it
991---     fits awkwardly there, so I'm leaving it here. It's
992---     optional anyway. We might consider assigning one of the
993---     exercises as advanced-only though.
994-
995--- A useless (though valid) Hoare triple:
996-
997---   {{ False }}  X := Y + 1  {{ X <= 5 }}
998-
999--- A better precondition:
1000-
1001---   {{ Y <= 4 /\ Z = 0 }}  X := Y + 1 {{ X <= 5 }}
1002-
1003--- The *best* precondition:
1004-
1005---   {{ Y <= 4 }}  X := Y + 1  {{ X <= 5 }}
1006-
1007--- Assertion `Y <= 4` is a *weakest precondition* of command
1008--- `X := Y + 1` with respect to postcondition `X <= 5`. Think
1009--- of *weakest* here as meaning "easiest to satisfy": a weakest
1010--- precondition is one that as many states as possible can
1011--- satisfy.
1012-
1013--- `P` is a weakest precondition of command `c` for
1014--- postcondition `Q` if
1015-
1016--- - `P` is a precondition, that is, `{{P}} c {{Q}}`; and
1017-
1018--- - `P` is at least as weak as all other preconditions, that is,
1019---   if `{{P'}} c {{Q}}` then `P' ->> P`.
1020-
1021--- Note that weakest preconditions need not be unique. For
1022--- example, `Y <= 4` was a weakest precondition above, but so
1023--- are the logically equivalent assertions `Y < 5`,
1024--- `Y <= 2 * 2`, etc. It is easy to show that any two weakest
1025--- preconditions `P` and `P'` of a command `c` with respect to
1026--- postcondition `Q` are logically equivalent; that is,
1027--- `P <<->> P'`.
1028-
1029-def IsWp (P : Assertion) (c : Com) (Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
1030-  ValidHoareTriple P c Q ∧
1031-  ∀ P' : Assertion, ValidHoareTriple P' c Q → P' ->> P
1032-

1039-
1040---   2) {{ ? }}  X := Y + Z {{ X = 5 }}
1041-
1042---   3) {{ ? }}  X := Y  {{ X = Y }}
1043-
1044---   4) {{ ? }}
1045---    if X = 0 then Y := Z + 1 else Y := W + 2 end
1046---    {{ Y = 5 }}
1047-
1048---   5) {{ ? }}
1049---    X := 5
1050---    {{ X = 0 }}
1051-
1052---   6) {{ ? }}
1053---    while true do X := 0 end
1054---    {{ X = 0 }}

32---     tour has been retooled here for Lean. The tactic
33---     combinators `try` and `repeat` (and the custom-tactic
34---     `macro`) are introduced in this chapter; `<;>` and
35---     `simp` were already introduced in Logical Foundations
36---     (`<;>` in `Induction`) so we use them freely and the
37---     `<;>` section below is a recap. For linear arithmetic we
38---     use `lia`; NOTE that LF currently introduces `omega`,
39---     not `lia`, so this needs to be reconciled volume-wide
40---     (either introduce `lia` in LF, or keep `omega`).
41-
42--- We concentrate here on defining the *syntax* and *semantics*
43--- of Imp; later in this volume we develop a theory of *program
44--- equivalence* and introduce *Hoare Logic*, a popular logic
45--- for reasoning about imperative programs.
46-
47--- ## Expressions With Variables
48-
49--- ### States
50-
51--- Since we'll want to look variables up to find out their
52--- current values, we'll use total maps from the `Maps`
53--- chapter. A *machine state* (or just *state*) represents the
54--- current values of all variables at some point in the
55--- execution of a program.
56-
57--- We give the type of variable identifiers a name, `Ident`.
58--- For now it is just `String`; naming it makes the intent
59--- clearer.
60-
61-open scoped MyGetElem
62-
63-abbrev Ident := String
64-abbrev State := TotalMap Ident Nat
65-
66--- ### Syntax
67-
68--- We can add variables to the arithmetic expressions we had
69--- before simply by including one more constructor. (This is a
70--- fresh `Aexp`, replacing the variable-free one from the
71--- *Slang* chapter.)
72-
73--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
74---     That should be a live chapter link.
75-
76-inductive Aexp where
77-  | num (n : Nat)
78-  | id (x : Ident)                -- NEW
79-  | plus (a1 a2 : Aexp)
80-  | minus (a1 a2 : Aexp)
81-  | mult (a1 a2 : Aexp)
82-
83--- Note to developers (Chris Henson @chenson2018):
84---     Rather than define identifiers as Ident, a more general
85---     approach is to use a **type variable** with
86---     `DecidableEq` (as the `Maps` chapter does), threaded
87---     through `Aexp`/`Bexp`/`Com`/`State`. Stashed for a
88---     future decision; the parameterized version would look
89---     like:
90---
91---     `inductive Aexp (V : Type) where
92---       | num (n : Nat)
93---       | id (x : V)
94---       | plus (a1 a2 : Aexp V)
95---       | minus (a1 a2 : Aexp V)
96---       | mult (a1 a2 : Aexp V)
97---     -- … then `Bexp V`, `Com V`, `abbrev State (V) [DecidableEq V] :=
98---     -- TotalMap V Nat`, and `[DecidableEq V]` wherever a lookup/update is
99---     -- performed.`
100-
101--- The `Bexp` definition is unchanged, except that it now
102--- refers to the new `Aexp`.
103-
104-inductive Bexp where
105-  | bool (b : Bool)
106-  | eq (a1 a2 : Aexp)
107-  | neq (a1 a2 : Aexp)
108-  | le (a1 a2 : Aexp)
109-  | gt (a1 a2 : Aexp)
110-  | not (b : Bexp)
111-  | and (b1 b2 : Bexp)
112-
113--- Defining a few variable names as shorthands will make
114--- examples easier to read.
115-
116-def W : Ident := "W"
117-def X : Ident := "X"
118-def Y : Ident := "Y"
119-def Z : Ident := "Z"

121--- ### Notations
122-
123-/-- Arithmetic expressions of Imp -/
124-declare_syntax_cat imp_aexp
125-/-- Numeric literal -/
126-syntax:max num : imp_aexp
127-/-- Variable reference -/
128-syntax:max ident : imp_aexp
129-/-- Addition -/
130-syntax:65 imp_aexp:65 " + " imp_aexp:66 : imp_aexp
131-/-- Subtraction -/
132-syntax:65 imp_aexp:65 " - " imp_aexp:66 : imp_aexp
133-/-- Multiplication -/
134-syntax:70 imp_aexp:70 " * " imp_aexp:71 : imp_aexp
135-/-- Parentheses for grouping -/
136-syntax "(" imp_aexp ")" : imp_aexp
137-/-- Escape to Lean -/
138-syntax:max "~" term:max : imp_aexp
139-
140-/-- Embed an Imp arithmetic expression into a Lean term -/
141-syntax:min "aexp " "{" imp_aexp "}" : term
142-
143-open Lean in
144-macro_rules
145-  | `(aexp { $n:num }) => `(Aexp.num $(quote n.getNat))
146-  | `(aexp { $x:ident }) => `(Aexp.id $x)
147-  | `(aexp { ~$e }) => pure e
148-  | `(aexp { $a + $b }) => `(Aexp.plus (aexp {$a}) (aexp {$b}))
149-  | `(aexp { $a - $b }) => `(Aexp.minus (aexp {$a}) (aexp {$b}))
150-  | `(aexp { $a * $b }) => `(Aexp.mult (aexp {$a}) (aexp {$b}))
151-  | `(aexp { ($a) }) => `(aexp {$a})

155-/-- Boolean expressions of Imp -/
156-declare_syntax_cat imp_bexp
157-/-- Boolean literal (`true` or `false`) -/
158-syntax:max ident : imp_bexp
159-/-- Equality of arithmetic expressions -/
160-syntax:50 imp_aexp:51 " = " imp_aexp:51 : imp_bexp
161-/-- Disequality of arithmetic expressions -/
162-syntax:50 imp_aexp:51 " ≠ " imp_aexp:51 : imp_bexp
163-/-- Less than or equal -/

165-/-- Greater than -/
166-syntax:50 imp_aexp:51 " > " imp_aexp:51 : imp_bexp
167-/-- Boolean negation -/
168-syntax:70 "¬ " imp_bexp:70 : imp_bexp
169-/-- Boolean conjunction -/
170-syntax:35 imp_bexp:36 " ∧ " imp_bexp:35 : imp_bexp
171-/-- Parentheses for grouping -/
172-syntax "(" imp_bexp ")" : imp_bexp
173-/-- Escape to Lean -/
174-syntax:max "~" term:max : imp_bexp
175-
176-/-- Embed an Imp boolean expression into a Lean term -/
177-syntax:min "bexp " "{" imp_bexp "}" : term

183-open Lean in
184-macro_rules
185-  | `(bexp { $x:ident }) =>
186-    match x.getId with
187-    | `true  => `(Bexp.bool true)
188-    | `false => `(Bexp.bool false)
189-    | _      => Macro.throwErrorAt x s!"expected 'true' or 'false', got '{x.getId}'"
190-  | `(bexp { ~$e }) => pure e
191-  | `(bexp { $a:imp_aexp = $b:imp_aexp }) => `(Bexp.eq (aexp {$a}) (aexp {$b}))
192-  | `(bexp { $a:imp_aexp ≠ $b:imp_aexp }) => `(Bexp.neq (aexp {$a}) (aexp {$b}))
193-  | `(bexp { $a:imp_aexp ≤ $b:imp_aexp }) => `(Bexp.le (aexp {$a}) (aexp {$b}))
194-  | `(bexp { $a:imp_aexp > $b:imp_aexp }) => `(Bexp.gt (aexp {$a}) (aexp {$b}))
195-  | `(bexp { ¬ $b:imp_bexp }) => `(Bexp.not (bexp {$b}))
196-  | `(bexp { $b1:imp_bexp ∧ $b2:imp_bexp }) => `(Bexp.and (bexp {$b1}) (bexp {$b2}))
197-  | `(bexp { ($b:imp_bexp) }) => `(bexp {$b})

208-namespace Imp.Delab
209-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr Parenthesizer
210-
211-/-- Re-inserts parentheses in `imp_aexp` output according to the grammar's precedences. -/
212-@[category_parenthesizer imp_aexp]
213-def imp_aexp.parenthesizer : CategoryParenthesizer | prec => do
214-  maybeParenthesize `imp_aexp true wrapParens prec <|
215-    parenthesizeCategoryCore `imp_aexp prec
216-where
217-  wrapParens (stx : Syntax) : Syntax := Unhygienic.run do
218-    let pstx ← `(($(⟨stx⟩)))
219-    return pstx.raw.setInfo (SourceInfo.fromRef stx)
220-
221-/-- Re-inserts parentheses in `imp_bexp` output according to the grammar's precedences. -/
222-@[category_parenthesizer imp_bexp]
223-def imp_bexp.parenthesizer : CategoryParenthesizer | prec => do
224-  maybeParenthesize `imp_bexp true wrapParens prec <|
225-    parenthesizeCategoryCore `imp_bexp prec
226-where
227-  wrapParens (stx : Syntax) : Syntax := Unhygienic.run do
228-    let pstx ← `(($(⟨stx⟩)))
229-    return pstx.raw.setInfo (SourceInfo.fromRef stx)
230-
231-/-- Tag freshly built syntax with the term info that Lean's pretty printer expects. -/
232-def annAsTerm {any} (stx : TSyntax any) : DelabM (TSyntax any) :=
233-  (⟨·⟩) <$> annotateTermInfo ⟨stx.raw⟩
234-
235-/-- Rebuild `imp_aexp` concrete syntax from an `Aexp` term. -/
236-partial def delabAexpInner : DelabM (TSyntax `imp_aexp) := do
237-  let e ← getExpr
238-  let stx ←
239-    match_expr e with
240-    | Aexp.num _ =>
241-      match (← withAppArg getExpr).nat? with
242-      | some v => pure ⟨Syntax.mkNumLit (toString v) |>.raw⟩
243-      | none   => `(imp_aexp| ~$(← withAppArg delab))
244-    | Aexp.id _ =>
245-      -- A variable reference like aexp { X } elaborates to Aexp.id X where X is the
246-      -- declared Ident constant, so the delaborators print the constant's name as a
247-      -- bare identifier (and also handle the .id "X" string-literal form).
248-      match ← withAppArg getExpr with
249-      | .const nm _      => `(imp_aexp| $(mkIdent nm):ident)
250-      | .lit (.strVal s) => `(imp_aexp| $(mkIdent (.mkSimple s)):ident)
251-      | _                => `(imp_aexp| ~$(← withAppArg delab))
252-    | Aexp.plus _ _ =>
253-      let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpInner
254-      let s2 ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
255-      `(imp_aexp| $s1 + $s2)
256-    | Aexp.minus _ _ =>
257-      let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpInner
258-      let s2 ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
259-      `(imp_aexp| $s1 - $s2)
260-    | Aexp.mult _ _ =>
261-      let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpInner
262-      let s2 ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
263-      `(imp_aexp| $s1 * $s2)
264-    | _ => `(imp_aexp| ~$(← delab))
265-  annAsTerm stx
266-
267-/-- Rebuild `imp_bexp` concrete syntax from a `Bexp` term. -/
268-partial def delabBexpInner : DelabM (TSyntax `imp_bexp) := do
269-  let e ← getExpr
270-  let stx ←
271-    match_expr e with
272-    | Bexp.bool _ =>
273-      match ← withAppArg getExpr with
274-      | .const ``Bool.true _  => `(imp_bexp| $(mkIdent `true):ident)
275-      | .const ``Bool.false _ => `(imp_bexp| $(mkIdent `false):ident)
276-      | _                     => `(imp_bexp| ~$(← withAppArg delab))
277-    | Bexp.eq _ _ =>
278-      let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpInner
279-      let s2 ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
280-      `(imp_bexp| $s1:imp_aexp = $s2:imp_aexp)
281-    | Bexp.neq _ _ =>
282-      let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpInner
283-      let s2 ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
284-      `(imp_bexp| $s1:imp_aexp ≠ $s2:imp_aexp)
285-    | Bexp.le _ _ =>
286-      let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpInner
287-      let s2 ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
288-      `(imp_bexp| $s1:imp_aexp ≤ $s2:imp_aexp)
289-    | Bexp.gt _ _ =>
290-      let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpInner
291-      let s2 ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
292-      `(imp_bexp| $s1:imp_aexp > $s2:imp_aexp)
293-    | Bexp.not _ =>
294-      let s ← withAppArg delabBexpInner
295-      `(imp_bexp| ¬ $s)
296-    | Bexp.and _ _ =>
297-      let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabBexpInner
298-      let s2 ← withAppArg delabBexpInner
299-      `(imp_bexp| $s1 ∧ $s2)
300-    | _ => `(imp_bexp| ~$(← delab))
301-  annAsTerm stx
302-
303--- END DETAILS
304-
305--- The `whenPPOption getPPNotation` wrapper lets
306--- `set_option pp.notation false` switch this delaborator off,
307--- revealing the raw constructors (see the "Desugaring
308--- Notations" discussion, after the commands are introduced).
309-
310--- THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: registering the delaborators
311-
312-@[delab app.Aexp.num, delab app.Aexp.id, delab app.Aexp.plus,
313-  delab app.Aexp.minus, delab app.Aexp.mult]
314-partial def delabAexp : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
315-  -- This delaborator only understands `Aexp`'s constructors -- bail otherwise.
316-  guard <| match_expr ← getExpr with
317-    | Aexp.num _ => true
318-    | Aexp.id _ => true
319-    | Aexp.plus _ _ => true
320-    | Aexp.minus _ _ => true
321-    | Aexp.mult _ _ => true
322-    | _ => false
323-  match ← delabAexpInner with
324-  | `(imp_aexp| ~$e) => pure e
325-  | e => `(term| aexp { $e })
326-
327-@[delab app.Bexp.bool, delab app.Bexp.eq, delab app.Bexp.neq, delab app.Bexp.le,
328-  delab app.Bexp.gt, delab app.Bexp.not, delab app.Bexp.and]
329-partial def delabBexp : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
330-  guard <| match_expr ← getExpr with
331-    | Bexp.bool _ => true
332-    | Bexp.eq _ _ => true
333-    | Bexp.neq _ _ => true
334-    | Bexp.le _ _ => true
335-    | Bexp.gt _ _ => true
336-    | Bexp.not _ => true
337-    | Bexp.and _ _ => true
338-    | _ => false
339-  match ← delabBexpInner with
340-  | `(imp_bexp| ~$e) => pure e
341-  | e => `(term| bexp { $e })
342-
343-end Imp.Delab
344-

355--- ### Evaluation
356-
357--- Now we need to add an `st` parameter to both evaluation
358--- functions:
359-
360-def Aexp.eval (st : State) (a : Aexp) : Nat :=
361-  match a with
362-  | num   n     =>  n
363-  | id    x     =>  st[x]                    -- NEW
364-  | plus  a1 a2 =>  a1.eval st + a2.eval st
365-  | minus a1 a2 =>  a1.eval st - a2.eval st
366-  | mult  a1 a2 =>  a1.eval st * a2.eval st
367-
368-def Bexp.eval (st : State) (b : Bexp) : Bool :=
369-  match b with
370-  | bool b      =>  b
371-  | eq   a1 a2  =>  a1.eval st == a2.eval st
372-  | neq  a1 a2  =>  a1.eval st != a2.eval st
373-  | le   a1 a2  =>  a1.eval st ≤  a2.eval st
374-  | gt   a1 a2  =>  a1.eval st >  a2.eval st
375-  | not  b1     =>  !b1.eval st
376-  | and  b1 b2  =>  b1.eval st && b2.eval st
377-
378-@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_num (st : State) (n : Nat) : (num n).eval st = n := rfl
379-@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_id (st : State) (x : Ident) : (Aexp.id x).eval st = st[x] := rfl
380-@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_plus (st : State) (a1 a2 : Aexp) :
381-    (plus a1 a2).eval st = a1.eval st + a2.eval st := rfl
382-@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_minus (st : State) (a1 a2 : Aexp) :
383-    (minus a1 a2).eval st = a1.eval st - a2.eval st := rfl
384-@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_mult (st : State) (a1 a2 : Aexp) :
385-    (mult a1 a2).eval st = a1.eval st * a2.eval st := rfl
386-
387-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_bool (st : State) (b : Bool) : (bool b).eval st = b := rfl
388-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_eq (st : State) (a1 a2 : Aexp) :
389-    (eq a1 a2).eval st = (a1.eval st == a2.eval st) := rfl
390-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_neq (st : State) (a1 a2 : Aexp) :
391-    (neq a1 a2).eval st = (a1.eval st != a2.eval st) := rfl
392-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_le (st : State) (a1 a2 : Aexp) :
393-    (le a1 a2).eval st = (a1.eval st ≤ a2.eval st : Bool) := rfl
394-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_gt (st : State) (a1 a2 : Aexp) :
395-    (gt a1 a2).eval st = (a1.eval st > a2.eval st : Bool) := rfl
396-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_not (st : State) (b : Bexp) : (not b).eval st = !b.eval st := rfl
397-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_and (st : State) (b1 b2 : Bexp) :
398-    (and b1 b2).eval st = (b1.eval st && b2.eval st) := rfl
399-
400--- We reuse the total-map notation (`x →ₜ v ; ∅` etc.) for
401--- states.
402-
403-example : aexp { 3 + (X * 2) }.eval (X →ₜ 5 ; ∅) = 13 := by rfl
404-
405-example : aexp { Z + (X * Y) }.eval (X →ₜ 5 ; Y →ₜ 4 ; ∅) = 20 := by rfl
406-
407-example : bexp { true ∧ ¬(X ≤ 4) }.eval (X →ₜ 5 ; ∅) = true := by rfl

416--- ## Commands
417-
418-inductive Com where
419-  | skip
420-  | asgn (x : Ident) (a : Aexp)
421-  | seq (c1 c2 : Com)
422-  | cond (b : Bexp) (c1 c2 : Com)
423-  | whileDo (b : Bexp) (c : Com)
424-
425--- THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: commands, macro rules
426-
427-/-- Imp commands -/
428-declare_syntax_cat imp_com
429-/-- The command that does nothing (`skip`) -/
430-syntax ident : imp_com
431-/-- Sequencing: one command after another -/
432-syntax imp_com ";" ppDedent(ppLine imp_com) : imp_com
433-/-- Assignment -/
434-syntax ident " := " imp_aexp : imp_com
435-/-- Conditional -/
436-syntax "if " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine imp_com ppDedent(ppLine "}" ppHardSpace "else" ppHardSpace "{") ppLine imp_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : imp_com
437-/-- Loop -/
438-syntax "while " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine imp_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : imp_com
439-/-- Escape to Lean -/
440-syntax:max "~" term:max : imp_com
441-
442-/-- Include an Imp command in Lean code -/
443-syntax:min "imp" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine imp_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : term
444-
445-namespace Com
446-
447-open Lean in
448-scoped macro_rules
449-  | `(imp { $x:ident }) =>
450-    if x.getId == `skip then `(Com.skip)
451-    else Macro.throwErrorAt x s!"expected 'skip', got '{x.getId}'"
452-  | `(imp { $c1 ; $c2 }) =>
453-    `(Com.seq (imp {$c1}) (imp {$c2}))
454-  | `(imp { $x:ident := $a }) =>
455-    `(Com.asgn $x (aexp {$a}))
456-  | `(imp { if ($b) {$c1} else {$c2} }) =>
457-    `(Com.cond (bexp {$b}) (imp {$c1}) (imp {$c2}))
458-  | `(imp { while ($b) {$c} }) =>
459-    `(Com.whileDo (bexp {$b}) (imp {$c}))
460-  | `(imp { ~$c }) =>
461-    pure c
462-
463-end Com
464-
465-open scoped Com
466-
467--- END DETAILS
