471-namespace Imp.Delab
472-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr
473-
474-partial def delabComInnerFor (ns : Name) (extra : DelabM (TSyntax `imp_com)) :
475-    DelabM (TSyntax `imp_com) := do
476-  let e ← getExpr
477-  let stx ←
478-    -- Using `(imp_com| skip)` would delaborate as `skip✝`. `mkIdent` fixes this.
479-    if e.isConstOf (ns ++ `skip) then
480-      `(imp_com| $(mkIdent `skip):ident)
481-    else if e.isAppOfArity (ns ++ `asgn) 2 then
482-      match ← withAppFn <| withAppArg getExpr with
483-      | .lit (.strVal s) =>
484-        let a ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
485-        `(imp_com| $(mkIdent (.mkSimple s)):ident := $a)
486-      | _ =>
487-        let `($x:ident) ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delab | failure
488-        let a ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
489-        `(imp_com| $x:ident := $a)
490-    else if e.isAppOfArity (ns ++ `seq) 2 then
491-      let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg (delabComInnerFor ns extra)
492-      let s2 ← withAppArg (delabComInnerFor ns extra)
493-      `(imp_com| $s1; $s2)
494-    else if e.isAppOfArity (ns ++ `cond) 3 then
495-      let b  ← withAppFn <| withAppFn <| withAppArg delabBexpInner
496-      let c1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg (delabComInnerFor ns extra)
497-      let c2 ← withAppArg (delabComInnerFor ns extra)
498-      `(imp_com| if ($b) {$c1} else {$c2})
499-    else if e.isAppOfArity (ns ++ `whileDo) 2 then
500-      let b ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabBexpInner
501-      let c ← withAppArg (delabComInnerFor ns extra)
502-      `(imp_com| while ($b) {$c})
503-    else
504-      extra <|> `(imp_com| ~$(← delab))
505-  annAsTerm stx
506-
507-/-- Rebuild `imp_com` concrete syntax from a `Com` term. -/
508-partial def delabComInner : DelabM (TSyntax `imp_com) :=
509-  delabComInnerFor ``Com failure
510-
511-@[delab app.Com.skip, delab app.Com.asgn, delab app.Com.seq,
512-  delab app.Com.cond, delab app.Com.whileDo]
513-partial def delabCom : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do

518-    | Com.cond _ _ _ => true

520-    | _ => false
521-  match ← delabComInner with

597--- ## Evaluating Commands

599--- ### Evaluation as a Function (Failed Attempt)
600-
601--- Here's an attempt at defining an evaluation function for
602--- commands (with a bogus `while` case).
603-
604-def Com.ceval_fun_no_while (st : State) (c : Com) : State :=
605-  match c with
606-  | imp {skip} => st
607-  | imp {x := ~a} => (x →ₜ a.eval st ; st)
608-  | imp {~c1; ~c2} =>
609-      let st' := ceval_fun_no_while st c1
610-      ceval_fun_no_while st' c2
611-  | imp {if (~b) {~c1} else {~c2}} =>
612-      if b.eval st then ceval_fun_no_while st c1
613-      else ceval_fun_no_while st c2
614-  | imp {while (~_) {~_}} => st     -- bogus

617---     Perhaps that discussion should be moved to -- or
618---     previewed in -- Logic.v? MRC'20: It's already in
619---     ProofObjects (which not everyone sees).

621--- A nonterminating
622--- `def loop_false (n) : False := loop_false n` would make
623--- `False` provable, so Lean rejects it.
624-
625--- ### Evaluation as a Relation
626-
627--- Here's a better way: define `ceval` as a *relation* rather
628--- than a *function* -- i.e., make its result a `Prop` rather
629--- than a `State`, similar to what we did for `Aexp.EvalR`
630--- above.
631-
632--- Note to developers (Michael Hicks @mwhicks1):
633---     I kind of hate this notation. Is there something more
634---     standard in Lean? CSLib precedent maybe?
635-
636--- We'll use the notation `st =[ c ]=> st'` for the `Com.EvalR`
637--- relation: `st =[ c ]=> st'` means that executing program `c`
638--- in a starting state `st` results in an ending state `st'`.
639--- This can be pronounced "`c` takes state `st` to `st'`".
640-
641--- Operational Semantics
642-
643--- Note to developers (before next release):
644---     BCP 21: I wonder if `seq` would be easier to work with
645---     if st' and st'' were swapped...
646-
647--- Here is an informal definition of evaluation, presented as
648--- inference rules for readability:
649-
650---                         -----------------                  (skip)
651---                         st =[ skip ]=> st
652-
653---                         a.eval st = n
654---                 --------------------------------           (asgn)
655---                 st =[ x := a ]=> (x →ₜ n ; st)
656-
657---                         st  =[ c1 ]=> st'
658---                         st' =[ c2 ]=> st''
659---                       ---------------------                (seq)
660---                       st =[ c1;c2 ]=> st''
661-
662---                        b.eval st = true
663---                         st =[ c1 ]=> st'
664---              --------------------------------------        (ifTrue)
665---              st =[ if b then c1 else c2 end ]=> st'
666-
667---                       b.eval st = false
668---                         st =[ c2 ]=> st'
669---              --------------------------------------        (ifFalse)
670---              st =[ if b then c1 else c2 end ]=> st'
671-
672---                       b.eval st = false
673---                  -----------------------------             (whileFalse)
674---                  st =[ while b do c end ]=> st
675-
676---                        b.eval st = true
677---                         st =[ c ]=> st'
678---                st' =[ while b do c end ]=> st''
679---                --------------------------------            (whileTrue)
680---                st  =[ while b do c end ]=> st''
681-
682--- Here is the formal definition. Make sure you understand how
683--- it corresponds to the inference rules.
684-
685--- Note to developers (Chris Henson @chenson2018):
686---     TODO Propose you use inline notation such as
687---     `Com.EvalR (imp {skip;}) st st`
688-
689-inductive Com.EvalR : Com → State → State → Prop where
690-  | skip {st : State} : EvalR (imp {skip}) st st
691-  | asgn {st : State} {a : Aexp} {n : Nat} {x : Ident} (h : a.eval st = n) :
692-      EvalR (imp {x := ~a}) st (x →ₜ n ; st)
693-  | seq {c1 c2 : Com} {st st' st'' : State} (h1 : EvalR c1 st st') (h2 : EvalR c2 st' st'') :
694-      EvalR (imp {~c1; ~c2}) st st''
695-  | ifTrue {st st' : State} {b : Bexp} {c1 c2 : Com} (hb : b.eval st = true)
696-      (hc : EvalR c1 st st') :
697-      EvalR (imp {if (~b) {~c1} else {~c2}}) st st'
698-  | ifFalse {st st' : State} {b : Bexp} {c1 c2 : Com} (hb : b.eval st = false)
699-      (hc : EvalR c2 st st') :
700-      EvalR (imp {if (~b) {~c1} else {~c2}}) st st'
701-  | whileFalse {b : Bexp} {st : State} {c : Com} (hb : b.eval st = false) :
702-      EvalR (imp {while (~b) {~c}}) st st
703-  | whileTrue {st st' st'' : State} {b : Bexp} {c : Com} (hb : b.eval st = true)
704-      (hc : EvalR c st st') (hloop : Com.EvalR (imp {while (~b) {~c}}) st' st'') :
705-      EvalR (imp {while (~b) {~c}}) st st''
706-

712-class HasEval (Com : Type) (In : outParam <| Type) (Out : outParam <| Type) where
713-  Eval : Com → In → Out → Prop

715-namespace HasEval
716-scoped notation:40 st0:41 " =[ " c " ]=> " st1:41 => Eval c st0 st1
717-

719--- be written without the `imp { … }` wrapper. Bare `Com` terms still work via the
720--- notation above; splice a Lean term into the command with `~`.
721-scoped syntax:40 term:41 " =[ " imp_com " ]=> " term:41 : term
722-scoped macro_rules
723-  | `($st0 =[ $c:imp_com ]=> $st1) => ``($st0 =[ imp { $c } ]=> $st1)
724-end HasEval

726-instance : HasEval Com State State where
727-  Eval := Com.EvalR

761--- The cost of defining evaluation as a relation instead of a
762--- function is that we now need to construct a *proof* that
763--- some program evaluates to some result state, rather than
764--- letting Lean's computation mechanism do it for us.

767-    ∅ =[
768-      X := 2;
769-      if (X ≤ 1) {
770-        Y := 3
771-      } else {
772-        Z := 4
773-      }
774-    ]=> (Z →ₜ 4 ; X →ₜ 2 ; ∅) := by
775-  -- We must supply the intermediate state.
776-  apply Com.EvalR.seq (st' := (X →ₜ 2 ; ∅))
777-  · apply Com.EvalR.asgn; rfl
778-  · apply Com.EvalR.ifFalse
779-    · rfl
780-    · apply Com.EvalR.asgn; rfl

853--- ### Determinism of Evaluation
854-
855--- Finally, we should pause to check that our evaluation
856--- relation really is a (partial) function...
857-
858-theorem ceval_deterministic (c : Com) (st st1 st2 : State)
859-    (e1 : st =[ c ]=> st1) (e2 : st =[ c ]=> st2) : st1 = st2 := by
860-  induction e1 generalizing st2 with
861-  | @skip st =>
862-      inversion e2
863-      rfl
864-  | @asgn st a n x h =>
865-      inversion e2 with
866-      | asgn h' => subst h; subst h'; rfl
867-  | @seq c1 c2 st st' st'' h1 h2 ih1 ih2 =>
868-      inversion e2 with
869-      | seq st2' h1' h2' =>
870-          have hst : st' = st2' := ih1 _ h1'
871-          subst hst
872-          exact ih2 _ h2'
873-  | @ifTrue st st' b c1 c2 hb hc ih =>
874-      inversion e2 with
875-      | ifTrue hb' hc' => exact ih _ hc'
876-      | ifFalse hb' hc' => simp_all
877-  | @ifFalse st st' b c1 c2 hb hc ih =>
878-      inversion e2 with
879-      | ifTrue hb' hc' => simp_all
880-      | ifFalse hb' hc' => exact ih _ hc'
881-  | @whileFalse b st c hb =>
882-      inversion e2 with
883-      | whileFalse hb' => rfl
884-      | whileTrue hb' hc' hl' => simp_all
885-  | @whileTrue st st' st'' b c hb hc hloop ih1 ih2 =>
886-      inversion e2 with
887-      | whileFalse hb' => simp_all
888-      | whileTrue st2' _ hc' hl' =>
889-          have hst : st' = st2' := ih1 _ hc'
890-          subst hst
891-          exact ih2 _ hl'

1-import SFLCompat
2-
3--- # Slang: Arithmetic and Boolean Expressions
4-
5--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
6---     We need to figure out our approach to text width,
7---     especially for proofs. Quite a few proofs here don't
8---     render into the chosen page width, and for terse mode it
9---     will be worse.
10-
11--- ## Arithmetic and Boolean Expressions
12-
13--- ### Syntax
14-
15-namespace Slang
16-
17--- Abstract syntax trees for arithmetic and boolean
18--- expressions:
19-
20-inductive Aexp where
21-  | num (n : Nat)
22-  | plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
23-  | minus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
24-  | mult (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
25-
26-inductive Bexp where
27-  | bool (b : Bool)
28-  | eq (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
29-  | neq (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
30-  | le (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
31-  | gt (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
32-  | not (b : Bexp)
33-  | and (b₁ b₂ : Bexp)
34-
35--- ### Evaluation
36-
37--- *Evaluating* an arithmetic expression produces a number.
38-
39-namespace Aexp
40-def eval (a : Aexp) : Nat :=
41-  match a with
42-  | num   n     =>  n
43-  | plus  a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval + a₂.eval
44-  | minus a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval - a₂.eval
45-  | mult  a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval * a₂.eval
46-
47-@[simp] theorem eval_num (n : Nat) : (num n).eval = n := rfl
48-@[simp] theorem eval_plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : (plus a₁ a₂).eval = a₁.eval + a₂.eval := rfl
49-@[simp] theorem eval_minus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : (minus a₁ a₂).eval = a₁.eval - a₂.eval := rfl
50-@[simp] theorem eval_mult (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : (mult a₁ a₂).eval = a₁.eval * a₂.eval := rfl
51-
52-example : eval (.plus (.num 2) (.num 2)) = 4 := by simp
53-end Aexp
54-
55--- Similarly, evaluating a boolean expression yields a boolean.
56-
57-namespace Bexp
58-def eval (b : Bexp) : Bool :=
59-  match b with
60-  | bool b     =>  b
61-  | eq   a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval == a₂.eval
62-  | neq  a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval != a₂.eval
63-  | le   a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval ≤ a₂.eval
64-  | gt   a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval > a₂.eval
65-  | not  b₁    =>  !eval b₁
66-  | and  b₁ b₂ =>  eval b₁ && eval b₂
67-
68-@[simp] theorem eval_bool (b : Bool) : (bool b).eval = b := rfl
69-@[simp] theorem eval_eq (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : (eq a₁ a₂).eval = (a₁.eval == a₂.eval) := rfl
70-@[simp] theorem eval_neq (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : (neq a₁ a₂).eval = (a₁.eval != a₂.eval) := rfl
71-@[simp] theorem eval_le (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : (le a₁ a₂).eval = (a₁.eval ≤ a₂.eval : Bool) := rfl
72-@[simp] theorem eval_gt (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : (gt a₁ a₂).eval = (a₁.eval > a₂.eval : Bool) := rfl
73-@[simp] theorem eval_not (b : Bexp) : (not b).eval = !b.eval := rfl
74-@[simp] theorem eval_and (b₁ b₂ : Bexp) : (and b₁ b₂).eval = (b₁.eval && b₂.eval) := rfl
75-end Bexp
76-
77--- It's worth noting that `≤` and `>` are `Prop`-valued, i.e.
78--- `a₁.eval st ≤ a₂.eval st` is a proposition, but `Bexp.eval`
79--- returns a `Bool`, so Lean implicitly inserts a `decide`
80--- coercion. You can observe the call to `decide` by hovering
81--- over `Bexp.eval_le` and `Bexp.eval_gt`.
82-
83--- _Quiz:_
84-
85--- What does the following expression evaluate to?
86-
87--- Aexp.eval (.plus (.num 3) (.minus (.num 4) (.num 1)))
88-
89--- (A) true (B) false (C) 0 (D) 3 (E) 6
90-
91--- ### Optimization
92-
93-def Aexp.optimize0plus (a : Aexp) : Aexp :=
94-  match a with
95-  | num   n          => num n
96-  | plus  (num 0) e₂ => optimize0plus e₂
97-  | plus  e₁      e₂ => plus  (optimize0plus e₁) (optimize0plus e₂)
98-  | minus e₁      e₂ => minus (optimize0plus e₁) (optimize0plus e₂)
99-  | mult  e₁      e₂ => mult  (optimize0plus e₁) (optimize0plus e₂)
100-
101-example :
102-    Aexp.optimize0plus (.plus (.num 2)
103-                               (.plus (.num 0)
104-                                      (.plus (.num 0) (.num 1))))
105-      = .plus (.num 2) (.num 1) := by rfl
106-
107-theorem optimize0plus_sound (a : Aexp) :
108-    a.optimize0plus.eval = a.eval := by
109-  induction a with
110-  | num n => rfl
111-  | plus a₁ a₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
112-    cases a₁ with
113-    | num n =>
114-      cases n with
115-      | zero =>
116-        simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_plus, Aexp.eval_num, Nat.zero_add]
117-        exact ih₂
118-      | succ n =>
119-        simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_plus, Aexp.eval_num]
120-        rw [ih₂]
121-    | plus b₁ b₂ =>
122-      simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_plus] at ih₁ ⊢
123-      rw [ih₁, ih₂]
124-    | minus b₁ b₂ =>
125-      simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_plus] at ih₁ ⊢
126-      rw [ih₁, ih₂]
127-    | mult b₁ b₂ =>
128-      simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_plus] at ih₁ ⊢
129-      rw [ih₁, ih₂]
130-  | minus a₁ a₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
131-    simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_minus]
132-    rw [ih₁, ih₂]
133-  | mult a₁ a₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
134-    simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_mult]
135-    rw [ih₁, ih₂]
136-
137--- We can use `fun_induction` to achieve a much shorter proof.
138-
139-theorem optimize0plus_sound' (a : Aexp) :
140-    a.optimize0plus.eval = a.eval := by
141-  fun_induction Aexp.optimize0plus a <;> simp_all
142-
143--- ### Exercise (3 stars): optimize0plusB_sound ⭐⭐⭐
144-
145--- Since the `Aexp.optimize0plus` transformation doesn't change
146--- the value of an `Aexp`, we should be able to apply it to all
147--- the `Aexp`s that appear in a `Bexp` without changing the
148--- `Bexp`'s value. Write a function that performs this
149--- transformation on `Bexp`s and prove it sound. Use the
150--- combinators we've just seen to make the proof as short and
151--- elegant as possible.
152-
153-def Bexp.optimize0plusB (b : Bexp) : Bexp := sorry
154-
155-theorem optimize0plusB_test1 :
156-    Bexp.optimize0plusB
157-        (.not (.gt (.plus (.num 0) (.num 4)) (.num 8)))
158-      = (.not (.gt (.num 4) (.num 8))) := sorry
159-
160-theorem optimize0plusB_test2 :
161-    Bexp.optimize0plusB
162-        (.and (.le (.plus (.num 0) (.num 4)) (.num 5)) (.bool true))
163-      = (.and (.le (.num 4) (.num 5)) (.bool true)) := sorry
164-
165-theorem optimize0plusB_sound (b : Bexp) :
166-    b.optimize0plusB.eval = b.eval := by
167-  sorry
168-
169--- ### Exercise (4 stars): optimize (Optional) ⭐⭐⭐⭐
170-
171--- The optimization implemented by our `Aexp.optimize0plus` is
172--- only one of many possible optimizations on arithmetic and
173--- boolean expressions. Write a more sophisticated optimizer
174--- and prove it correct. (You will probably find it easiest to
175--- start small -- add just a single, simple optimization and
176--- its correctness proof -- and build up incrementally to
177--- something more interesting.)
178-
179--- ## Evaluation as a Relation
180-
181-inductive Aexp.EvalR : Aexp → Nat → Prop where
182-  | num (n : Nat) : EvalR (.num n) n
183-  | plus {a₁ a₂ : Aexp} {n₁ n₂ : Nat} (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
184-      EvalR (.plus a₁ a₂) (n₁ + n₂)
185-  | minus {a₁ a₂ : Aexp} {n₁ n₂ : Nat} (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
186-      EvalR (.minus a₁ a₂) (n₁ - n₂)
187-  | mult {a₁ a₂ : Aexp} {n₁ n₂ : Nat} (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
188-      EvalR (.mult a₁ a₂) (n₁ * n₂)
189-
190--- One comment on the style of this definition. We could
191--- instead have presented this relation with **positional**
192--- hypotheses -- no names for the premises.
193-
194-namespace ArithUnnamed
195-
196-inductive Aexp.EvalR : Aexp → Nat → Prop where
197-  | num (n : Nat) : EvalR (.num n) n
198-  | plus {a₁ a₂ : Aexp} {n₁ n₂ : Nat} : EvalR a₁ n₁ → EvalR a₂ n₂ → EvalR (.plus a₁ a₂) (n₁ + n₂)
199-  | minus {a₁ a₂ : Aexp} {n₁ n₂ : Nat} : EvalR a₁ n₁ → EvalR a₂ n₂ → EvalR (.minus a₁ a₂) (n₁ - n₂)
200-  | mult {a₁ a₂ : Aexp} {n₁ n₂ : Nat} : EvalR a₁ n₁ → EvalR a₂ n₂ → EvalR (.mult a₁ a₂) (n₁ * n₂)
201-
202-end ArithUnnamed
203-
204--- It will be convenient to have an infix notation for
205--- `Aexp.EvalR`. We'll write `e ⇓ n` to mean that arithmetic
206--- expression `e` evaluates to value `n`. The `⇓` symbol is
207--- typed `\Downarrow`.
208-
209-scoped notation:55 e:56 " ⇓ " n:56 => Aexp.EvalR e n
210-

236-

239---     | bool b     => b

241---     | neq  a₁ a₂ => a₁.eval != a₂.eval
242---     | le   a₁ a₂ => a₁.eval ≤ a₂.eval

250--- ### Equivalence of the Definitions
251-
252--- It is straightforward to prove that the relational and
253--- functional definitions of evaluation agree.
254-
255-theorem Aexp.evalR_iff_eval (a : Aexp) (n : Nat) :
256-    a ⇓ n ↔ a.eval = n := by
257-  constructor
258-  · intro h
259-    induction h with
260-    | num n => rfl
261-    | plus h₁ h₂ ih₁ ih₂ => simp only [Aexp.eval_plus]; rw [ih₁, ih₂]
262-    | minus h₁ h₂ ih₁ ih₂ => simp only [Aexp.eval_minus]; rw [ih₁, ih₂]
263-    | mult h₁ h₂ ih₁ ih₂ => simp only [Aexp.eval_mult]; rw [ih₁, ih₂]
264-  · intro h
265-    subst h
266-    induction a with
267-    | num n => exact .num n
268-    | plus a₁ a₂ ih₁ ih₂ => exact .plus ih₁ ih₂
269-    | minus a₁ a₂ ih₁ ih₂ => exact .minus ih₁ ih₂
270-    | mult a₁ a₂ ih₁ ih₂ => exact .mult ih₁ ih₂
271-
272--- We can make the proof quite a bit shorter using more
273--- automation like we did in the previous section.
274-
275-theorem Aexp.evalR_iff_eval' (a : Aexp) (n : Nat) :
276-    a ⇓ n ↔ a.eval = n := by
277-  sorry

295-
296--- ### Computational vs. Relational Definitions
297-
298--- Sometimes relational definitions are the only reasonable
299--- option...
300-
301-namespace Slang.AevalRDivision
302-
303--- For example, suppose that we wanted to extend the arithmetic
304--- operations with division:
305-
306-inductive Aexp where
307-  | num (n : Nat)
308-  | plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
309-  | minus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
310-  | mult (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
311-  | div (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)             -- NEW
312-
313--- Extending the definition of `Aexp.eval` to handle this new
314--- operation would not be straightforward due to division being
315--- a *partial* operation; i.e., what should we return as the
316--- result of `.div (.num 5) (.num 0)`? One option would be to
317--- lift the definition of `Aexp.eval` to return an option:
318-
319-namespace Aexp
320-
321-def eval (a : Aexp) : Option Nat :=
322-  match a with
323-  | num   n     =>  some n
324-  | plus  a₁ a₂ =>  match a₁.eval, a₂.eval with
325-                    | some n₁, some n₂ => some (n₁ + n₂)
326-                    | _, _ => none
327-  | minus a₁ a₂ =>  match a₁.eval, a₂.eval with
328-                    | some n₁, some n₂ => some (n₁ - n₂)
329-                    | _, _ => none
330-  | mult  a₁ a₂ =>  match a₁.eval, a₂.eval with
331-                    | some n₁, some n₂ => some (n₁ * n₂)
332-                    | _, _ => none
333-  | div   a₁ a₂ =>  match a₁.eval, a₂.eval with
334-                    | _, some 0 => none
335-                    | some n₁, some n₂ => some (n₁ * n₂)
336-                    | _, _ => none
337-end Aexp
338-
339--- This definition is a lot wordier than the earlier version.
340--- There are tools to reduce this overhead, namely monads, but
341--- we will not discuss these in Software Foundations in Lean.
342--- Curious readers can learn more about them from [Functional
343--- Programming in
344--- Lean](https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Monads/).
345-
346--- By contrast, partiality is no problem for the relational
347--- version of the definition.
348-
349--- What should `Aexp.eval` return for
350--- `.div (.num 1) (.num 0)`??
351-
352-inductive Aexp.EvalR : Aexp → Nat → Prop where
353-  | num (n : Nat) : EvalR (.num n) n
354-  | plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
355-      EvalR (.plus a₁ a₂) (n₁ + n₂)
356-  | minus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
357-      EvalR (.minus a₁ a₂) (n₁ - n₂)
358-  | mult (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
359-      EvalR (.mult a₁ a₂) (n₁ * n₂)
360-  | div (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ n₃ : Nat)             -- NEW
361-      (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) (hpos : n₂ > 0) (hdiv : n₂ * n₃ = n₁) :
362-      EvalR (.div a₁ a₂) n₃
363-
364--- Notice that there are some inputs (those with a divisor of
365--- 0) for which this relation does not specify an output.
366-
367-end Slang.AevalRDivision
368-
369-namespace Slang.AevalRExtended
370-
371--- Another example: a *nondeterministic* number generator:
372-
373--- As another example, suppose that we want to extend the
374--- arithmetic operations by a nondeterministic number generator
375--- `any` that, when evaluated, may yield any number. (This is
376--- not the same as making a *probabilistic* choice among all
377--- numbers -- we only say which results are *possible*.)
378-
379-inductive Aexp where
380-  | any                            -- NEW
381-  | num (n : Nat)
382-  | plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
383-  | minus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
384-  | mult (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
385-
386--- Again, extending `Aexp.eval` would be tricky, since
387--- evaluation is now *not* a deterministic function from
388--- expressions to numbers; but extending the relation is no
389--- problem.
390-
391--- What should `Aexp.eval` do with nondeterminism??
392-
393--- h₂
394-
395-inductive Aexp.EvalR : Aexp → Nat → Prop where
396-  | any (n : Nat) : EvalR .any n                   -- NEW
397-  | num (n : Nat) : EvalR (.num n) n
398-  | plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
399-      EvalR (.plus a₁ a₂) (n₁ + n₂)
400-  | minus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
401-      EvalR (.minus a₁ a₂) (n₁ - n₂)
402-  | mult (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
403-      EvalR (.mult a₁ a₂) (n₁ * n₂)
404-
405-end Slang.AevalRExtended
406-
407--- Functional: computation. Relational: expressive. Best: both,
408--- proved equivalent.
409-

LF/CustomTactics.lean

1-module
2-
3-public meta import Lean.Elab.ConfigEval
4-public meta import Lean.Elab.Tactic.RenameInaccessibles
5-public meta import Lean.Elab.Tactic.Induction
6-meta import all Lean.Meta.Tactic.Cases
7-
8-meta section
9-
10-namespace Lean.Parser
11-open Tactic
12-
13-/-- Internal syntactic representation of a single inversion alternative. -/
14-declare_syntax_cat invAlt
15-syntax " | " caseArg " => " tacticSeq : invAlt
16-
17-/-- An inversion alternative matching one or more goal tags,
18-  expanding to multiple single [invAlt]s. -/
19-declare_syntax_cat invAlts
20-syntax (" | " caseArg)+ " => " tacticSeq : invAlts
21-
22-/--
23-  `inversion t` generalizes nonvariable indices of the type of `t` before invoking `cases t`,
24-  then solves away contradictory generated goals.
25-  `t` itself will also be generalized with a heterogeneous equality `heq`
26-  if trying to generalize the indices produces an ill-typed result.
27-  * If `inversion +clear t` is set, then `heq` will be `clear`ed from the context if present,
28-    along with `t` if there are no dependencies on it.
29-  * The form `inversion t with (tac ...) | tag₁ x ... => tac ... | ... | tagₙ z ... => tac ...`
30-    is supported, similar to that of `cases` and `inversion`.
31--/
32-syntax (name := inversion)
33-  "inversion " optConfig ident (" with " (tacticSeq)? (colGe invAlts)*)? : tactic
34-
35-end Lean.Parser
36-
37-namespace Lean.Meta
38-
39-/-- Get the user-facing name for the given metavariable. -/
40-def _root_.Lean.MVarId.getUserName (mvarId : MVarId) : MetaM Name := do
41-  let decl ← mvarId.getDecl
42-  return decl.userName
43-
44-/-- Get the string suffix of a name as a name -/
45-def _root_.Lean.Name.getSuffix : Name → Name
46-| .anonymous => .anonymous
47-| .str _ s => .str .anonymous s
48-| .num n _ => n.getSuffix
49-
50-/--
51-  This function is similar to `forallMetaTelescopeReducing`: Given `e` of the
52-  form `forall ..xs, A`, this combinator will create a new metavariable for
53-  each `x` in `xs` until it reaches an `x` whose type is defeq to `t`,
54-  and instantiate `A` with these, while also reducing `A` if needed.
55-  It uses `forallMetaTelescopeReducing`.
56-
57-  This function returns a triple `(mvs, bis, out)` where
58-  - `mvs` is an array containing the new metavariables.
59-  - `bis` is an array containing the binder infos for the `mvs`.
60-  - `out` is `e` but instantiated with the `mvs`.
61-
62-  Lifted from [https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/master/Mathlib/Lean/Meta/Basic.lean#L41].
63--/
64-def forallMetaTelescopeReducingUntilDefEq
65-    (e t : Expr) (kind : MetavarKind := MetavarKind.natural) :
66-    MetaM (Array Expr × Array BinderInfo × Expr) := do
67-  let (ms, bs, tp) ← forallMetaTelescopeReducing e (some 1) kind
68-  unless ms.size == 1 do
69-    if ms.size == 0 then throwError m!"Failed: {← ppExpr e} is not the type of a function."
70-    else throwError m!"Failed"
71-  let mut mvs := ms
72-  let mut bis := bs
73-  let mut out : Expr := tp
74-  while !(← isDefEq (← inferType mvs.toList.getLast!) t) do
75-    let (ms, bs, tp) ← forallMetaTelescopeReducing out (some 1) kind
76-    unless ms.size == 1 do
77-      throwError m!"Failed to find {← ppExpr t} as the type of a parameter of {← ppExpr e}."
78-    mvs := mvs ++ ms
79-    bis := bis ++ bs
80-    out := tp
81-  return (mvs, bis, out)
82-
83-/-- Given equations `eqs` in the local context of `mvarId`,
84-  unify them using [Lean.Meta.unifyEq?],
85-  but if unification fails, leave the equation in the context.
86-  This means we should never get a "Dependent elimination failed" error.
87-  While marked partial, this _should_ always terminate,
88-  decreasing on the sum of the sizes of the terms of each equation.
89-
90-  Lifted from [Lean.Meta.Cases.unifyEqs]. -/
91-partial def unifyEqs (eqs : List FVarId) (mvarId : MVarId) (subst : FVarSubst) (caseName? : Option Name) : MetaM (MVarId × FVarSubst) := withIncRecDepth do
92-  match eqs with
93-  | [] => return (mvarId, subst)
94-  | eq :: eqs =>
95-    let some { mvarId, subst, numNewEqs } ← Option.join <$> (observing? $ unifyEq? mvarId eq subst MVarId.acyclic caseName?)
96-      | unifyEqs eqs mvarId subst caseName?
97-    let (newEqs, mvarId) ← mvarId.introN numNewEqs
98-    let eqs := eqs.map (Expr.fvarId! ∘ subst.get)
99-    unifyEqs (newEqs.toList ++ eqs) mvarId subst caseName?
100-
101-/-- Lifted from [Lean.Meta.Cases.unifyCasesEqs]. -/
102-def unifyCasesEqs (eqs : List FVarId) (subgoals : Array CasesSubgoal) : MetaM (Array CasesSubgoal) :=
103-  subgoals.filterMapM fun s => do
104-    let eqs := eqs.filterMap (Expr.fvarId? ∘ s.subst.get)
105-    let (mvarId, subst) ← unifyEqs eqs s.mvarId s.subst s.ctorName
106-    if (← mvarId.isAssignedOrDelayedAssigned) then return none
107-    else return some { s with
108-      mvarId := mvarId,
109-      subst  := subst,
110-      fields := s.fields.map (subst.apply ·)
111-    }
112-
113-/-- Try to clear the given fvars from the local context of each subgoal,
114-  using the subgoals' substitution mappings to find the fvars.
115-
116-  As with [MVarId.tryClearMany], the fvars must be in the order they appear in the context.  -/
117-def casesClearMany (subgoals : Array CasesSubgoal) (fvarIds : Array FVarId) : MetaM (Array CasesSubgoal) :=
118-  subgoals.mapM fun s => do
119-    let fvarIds := fvarIds.filterMap (Expr.fvarId? ∘ s.subst.get)
120-    let mvarId ← s.mvarId.tryClearMany fvarIds
121-    return { s with mvarId }
122-
123-end Lean.Meta
124-
125-namespace Lean.Elab.Tactic
126-open Meta Term
127-
128--- [https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/master/Mathlib/Tactic/Lemma.lean]
129--- [https://github.com/leanprover-community/batteries/blob/main/Batteries/Tactic/Lemma.lean]
130-/-- Synonym for `theorem`. -/
131-macro "lemma " thm:declId sig:declSig val:declVal : command => `(theorem $thm $sig $val)
132-
133-/--
134-  `apply t at i` uses forward reasoning with `t` at the hypothesis `i`.
135-  Explicitly, if `t : α₁ → ⋯ → αᵢ → ⋯ → αₙ` and `i` has type `αᵢ`, then this tactic adds
136-  metavariables/goals for any terms of `αⱼ` for `j = 1, …, i-1`,
137-  then replaces the type of `i` with `αᵢ₊₁ → ⋯ → αₙ` by applying those metavariables and the
138-  original `i`.
139-
140-  Lifted from [https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/master/Mathlib/Tactic/ApplyAt.lean].
141--/
142-elab "apply " t:term " at " i:ident : tactic => withSynthesize <| withMainContext do
143-  let f ← elabTermForApply t
144-  let some ldecl := (← getLCtx).findFromUserName? i.getId
145-    | throwErrorAt i m!"Identifier {i} not found"
146-  let (mvs, bis, _) ← forallMetaTelescopeReducingUntilDefEq (← inferType f) ldecl.type
147-  for (m, b) in mvs.zip bis do
148-    if b.isInstImplicit && !(← m.mvarId!.isAssigned) then
149-      try m.mvarId!.inferInstance
150-      catch _ => continue
151-  let (_, mainGoal) ← (← getMainGoal).note ldecl.userName
152-    (← mkAppOptM' f (mvs.pop.push ldecl.toExpr |>.map some))
153-  let mainGoal ← mainGoal.tryClear ldecl.fvarId
154-  replaceMainGoal <| [mainGoal] ++ mvs.pop.toList.map (·.mvarId!)
155-
156-structure InversionConfig where
157-  clear : Bool := false
158-
159-declare_config_elab elabInversionConfig InversionConfig
160-
161-open Cases in
162-def inversionCore (h : FVarId) (config : InversionConfig) : TacticM (List MVarId) := withMainContext do
163-  let goal ← getMainGoal
164-  goal.withContext do
165-    let some ctx ← mkCasesContext? h
166-    | throwTacticEx `inversion goal "Target {Expr.fvar h} does not belong to an inductive type"
167-    -- If the target's type isn't a predicate with indices, behave like `cases`
168-    if ← hasIndepIndices ctx then
169-      let subgoals ← inductionCasesOn goal h default ctx
170-      let subgoals ← if config.clear
171-        then casesClearMany subgoals #[h]
172-        else pure subgoals
173-      subgoals.toList.mapM setUserName
174-    -- Otherwise, use custom [unifyEqs] to not fail on unifying HEqs
175-    else
176-      let gis@⟨newGoal, _, newTarget, numEqs⟩ ← generalizeIndices goal h
177-      let (newEqs, newGoal) ← newGoal.introN numEqs
178-      let some targetEq := newEqs.back?
179-      | throwTacticEx `inversion newGoal "Failed to generalize target"
180-      let subgoals ← inductionCasesOn newGoal newTarget default ctx
181-      let subgoals ← elimAuxIndices gis subgoals
182-      let subgoals ← unifyCasesEqs newEqs.toList subgoals
183-      let subgoals ← if config.clear
184-        then casesClearMany subgoals #[h, targetEq]
185-        else pure subgoals
186-      subgoals.toList.mapM setUserName
187-  where
188-    setUserName (subgoal : CasesSubgoal) : TacticM MVarId := do
189-      if let some name := subgoal.ctorName then
190-        subgoal.mvarId.setUserName name.getSuffix
191-      return subgoal.mvarId
192-
193-/-- Given an inversion alternative and a list of goals,
194-  solve the tagged goal with the provided tactics,
195-  throwing an error if the goal cannot be found or solved. -/
196-def evalInvAlt (goals : List MVarId) (alt : TSyntax `invAlt) : TacticM (List MVarId) :=
197-  match alt with
198-  | `(invAlt| | $tag:ident $vars:binderIdent* => $tactics:tacticSeq) => do
199-    if let some goal ← goals.findM? (matchTag tag.getId <$> ·.getUserName) then
200-      return [← trySolveGoal vars tactics goal]
201-    else throwError m!"Invalid alternative name `{tag.getId}`: {← errorMsg}"
202-  | `(invAlt| | _ $vars:binderIdent* => $tactics:tacticSeq) => do
203-    if !goals.isEmpty then
204-      goals.mapM (trySolveGoal vars tactics)
205-    else throwErrorAt alt m!"Invalid wildcard alternative: {← errorMsg}"
206-  | _ => throwErrorAt alt "Could not parse inversion alternative"
207-where
208-  matchTag tag name : Bool :=
209-    tag == name || tag.isPrefixOf name || tag.isSuffixOf name
210-  trySolveGoal vars tactics goal : TacticM MVarId := do
211-    let goals ← renameInaccessibles goal vars >>= evalTacticAt tactics
212-    unless goals.isEmpty do
213-      reportUnsolvedGoals goals
214-    return goal
215-  errorMsg : TacticM MessageData := do
216-    let goalMsgs ← goals.mapM (.ofName <$> ·.getUserName)
217-    return if goals.isEmpty
218-      then m!"There are no unhandled alternatives"
219-      else m!"Expected {.orList goalMsgs}"
220-
221-@[tactic Lean.Parser.inversion, inherit_doc Lean.Parser.inversion]
222-public meta def evalInversion : Tactic
223-  | `(tactic| inversion $config $h:ident $[with $[$tactics?:tacticSeq]? $[$alts?:invAlts]*]?) => do
224-    let config ← elabInversionConfig config
225-    let mut goals ← inversionCore (← getFVarId h) config
226-    if let some tactics := tactics?.join then
227-      let subgoals ← goals.mapM (evalTacticAt tactics)
228-      goals ← subgoals.flatten.filterM (not <$> ·.isAssignedOrDelayedAssigned)
229-    if let some alts := alts? then
230-      let expandedAlts ← Array.flatten <$> alts.mapM expandInvAlts
231-      for alt in expandedAlts do
232-        let solvedGoals ← evalInvAlt goals alt
233-        goals := goals.filter (!solvedGoals.contains ·)
234-      unless goals.isEmpty do
235-        reportUnsolvedGoals goals
236-    replaceMainGoal goals
237-  | stx => throwErrorAt stx "Could not parse inversion tactic"
238-where expandInvAlts
239-  | `(invAlts| $[| $args:caseArg]* => $tactics:tacticSeq) =>
240-    args.mapM (`(invAlt| | $(·) => $tactics))
241-  | stx => throwErrorAt stx "Could not parse inversion alternatives"
242-
243-end Lean.Elab.Tactic
244-
245-end -- meta section

247-namespace Tests
248-open Nat
249-
250-set_option autoImplicit false
251-set_option pp.proofs true
252-set_option pp.fieldNotation false
253-
254-/-! # `inversion` tests -/
255-
256-/-- In Lean, "inversion" on `leq : f n ≤ 0`, where `f : Nat → Nat`,
257-  requires `generalizing e : f n = m`, since Lean does not perform
258-  the dependent case analysis automatically. `cases leq` will fail here.
259-  We want to keep the style of reasoning familiar to PL:
260-  "I know `h`; what must have been true for `h` to be true?"
261-  The technicality of needing to generalize hinders teaching and learning
262-  this style of reasoning for audiences new to proof assistants and logic.
263-  To solve this, we introduce and use the `inversion` tactic,
264-  which automatically generalizes varaibles, performs case analysis,
265-  and eliminates impossible subcases. -/
266-example (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ 0) : 0 = f n := by
267-  -- cases leq /- Dependent elimination failed: Failed to solve equation 0 = f n -/
268-  inversion leq; assumption
269-
270-example (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ 0) : 0 = f n := by
271-  inversion +clear leq; assumption
272-
273-/-- error: Unknown identifier `leq` -/
274-#guard_msgs(error) in
275-example (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ 0) : 0 = f n := by
276-  inversion +clear leq
277-  guard_hyp leq
278-
279-example (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ 0) : 0 = f n := by
280-  inversion leq with
281-  | refl heq eq =>
282-    guard_hyp heq : leq ≍ le.refl
283-    guard_hyp eq : 0 = f n
284-    assumption
285-
286-/-- warning: declaration uses `sorry` -/
287-#guard_msgs(warning) in
288-example (f : Nat → Nat) (n m : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ f m) : f n = 0 := by
289-  inversion leq with
290-  | refl e _ | step k _ e _ =>
291-    try rw [← e]
292-    sorry
293-
294-/-- error: Invalid wildcard alternative: There are no unhandled alternatives -/
295-#guard_msgs(error) in
296-example (f : Nat → Nat) (n m : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ f m) : f n = 0 := by
297-  inversion +clear leq with
298-  | refl e | step k _ e =>
299-    try rw [← e]
300-    sorry
301-  | _ => sorry
302-
303-/-- error: Invalid alternative name `step`: There are no unhandled alternatives -/
304-#guard_msgs(error) in
305-example (f : Nat → Nat) (n m : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ f m) : f n = 0 := by
306-  inversion +clear leq with
307-  | _ e | step k _ e =>
308-    try rw [← e]
309-    sorry
310-
311-inductive The : ∀ {α}, α → Prop where
312-  | mk : The zero
313-
314-/-- sfl#40: Case names should be the constructors' names -/
315-example {x : Nat} (h : The x) : x = zero := by
316-  inversion h with
317-  | mk => rfl
318-
319-example {α} {n m k : α} : [n, m] = [k, k] → [n] = [m] := by
320-  intro h
321-  inversion h; rfl
322-
323-example {n : Nat} : n + 1 = 1 + n := by
324-  induction n with try rfl
325-  | succ => lia
326-
327-inductive NoStutter {α : Type} : List α → Prop where
328-  | nostutter0: NoStutter []
329-  | nostutter1 {n} : NoStutter (n :: [])
330-  | nostutter2 {x y l} (hneq : x ≠ y) (h : NoStutter (y :: l)) : NoStutter (x :: y :: l)
331-
332-/-- The last (only) case name need not be provided -/
333-example : ¬ (NoStutter [3, 1, 1, 4]) := by
334-  intro contra
335-  inversion contra with | _ contra =>
336-  inversion contra with | _ h _ =>
337-  apply h
338-  rfl
339-
340-/-- Inversion may optionally take a sequence of tactics on all goals -/
341-example {α x y} {l : List α} (h : NoStutter l) (hl : l = x :: y :: []) : x ≠ y := by
342-  inversion h with
343-    injections
344-    try subst_vars
345-  | nostutter2 => assumption
346-
347-/-- `with` acts similarly to `<;>` on the optional sequence of tactics -/
348-example {α x y} {l : List α} (h : NoStutter l) (hl : l = x :: y :: []) : x ≠ y := by
349-  inversion h with
350-    injections
351-    try (subst_vars; assumption)
352-
353-example {x y} {l : List Nat} (h : NoStutter l) (hl : l = x :: y :: []) : x ≠ y := by
354-  inversion h with
355-    injections
356-    try cases x
357-  | nostutter2.zero => subst_vars; assumption
358-  | nostutter2.succ => subst_vars; assumption
359-
360-inductive Vec α : Nat → Type where
361-  | nil : Vec α 0
362-  | cons {n} : α → Vec α n → Vec α (n + 1)
363-
364-/-- Inversion should work on indexed `Type`s as well -/
365-example {α} (n : Nat) (v : Vec α (n + 1)) : ∃ hd tl, v = Vec.cons hd tl := by
366-  inversion v with
367-  | cons hd tl => exists hd, tl
368-
369-inductive Wec α : Nat → Type where
370-  | nil : Wec α 0
371-  | cons {n} (f : Nat → Nat) : α → Wec α n → Wec α (f n)
372-
373-/-- warning: declaration uses `sorry` -/
374-#guard_msgs(warning) in
375-example {α} (n : Nat) (v : Wec α (succ n)) :
376-    ∃ hd tl, v = Wec.cons succ hd tl := by
377-  inversion v with
378-  | cons m f hd tl eq heq =>
379-    guard_hyp eq : succ n = f m
380-    guard_hyp heq : v ≍ Wec.cons f hd tl
381-    sorry
382-
383-inductive EmptyRelation : Nat → Nat → Prop where
384-
385-/-- sfl#52: Inversion should still work on nonindexed `Prop`s -/
386-example n m : ¬ EmptyRelation n m := by
387-  intro contra; inversion contra
388-
389-/-- With `inductive.autoPromoteIndices` true (the default),
390-  this is also a nonindexed `Prop`... -/
391-inductive silly : Nat → Prop where
392-| silly1 n (h : n > 1) : silly n
393-| silly2 n (h : exists m, m * 2 = n) : silly n
394-| silly3 n (h : exists m, n = m + 2) : silly n
395-
396-/-- ...and inversion should continue to work -/
397-example {n} (h : silly n) : n ≠ 1 := by
398-  inversion h <;> omega
399-
400-/-- Inversion should also work on nonindexed `Type`s -/
401-example (n : Nat) : Nat := by
402-  inversion n with
403-  | zero => exact zero
404-  | succ n' => exact n'
405-
406-/-! # `lemma` tests -/
407-
408-lemma doubleNegation : ∀ P, P → ¬ ¬ P := by
409-  intro P p np; exact (np p)
410-
411-/-! # `apply` tests -/
412-
413-example (H : Bool → Nat → False) (n : Nat) : False := by
414-  apply H at n; apply n; exact true
415-
416-end Tests

LF/Typeclasses.lean

1-import SFLCompat
2-
3--- # Typeclasses
4-
5--- Chapter Poly introduced **parametric polymorphism**,
6--- declaring a type variable with no constraint on it.
7-
8--- Note to developers (Michael Hicks @mwhicks1):
9---     Students will run across universes, though. When looking
10---     at List lemmas, for example, they will see things like:
11---
12---     `List.reverse.{u} {α : Type u} (as : List α) : List α`
13---
14---     Are we explaining these things somewhere, maybe in Poly
15---     ?
16-
17--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
18---     Yes, in Poly!
19-
20--- This lets us work with a type like `List α`, writing
21--- functions like `List.reverse` and `List.length` and proofs
22--- like `List.length_reverse`, which use only the list's
23--- structure and never inspect any particular `a : α`.
24-
25--- Sometimes, though, we want less freedom: rather than leaving
26--- `α` completely generic, we want to partially specify its
27--- behavior. In Lean, this is done through a form of "ad hoc
28--- polymorphism" called **typeclasses**. The concept originated
29--- in Haskell and is analogous to features you may know from
30--- other languages, such as traits in Rust.
31-
32--- ## Why We Need Typeclasses
33-
34--- Consider the following function, which checks whether a
35--- natural number occurs in a list:
36-
37-def List.elem_nat (a : Nat) (xs : List Nat) : Bool :=
38-  match xs with
39-  | [] => false
40-  | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_nat a tl
41-
42-theorem List.elem_nat_nil (a : Nat) : [].elem_nat a = false := rfl
43-
44-theorem List.elem_nat_cons (a b : Nat) (xs : List Nat) :
45-    (b :: xs).elem_nat a = bif a == b then true else elem_nat a xs := rfl
46-
47-#eval [0, 1].elem_nat 0
48-#eval [0, 1].elem_nat 1
49-#eval [0, 1].elem_nat 2
50-
51--- What if we want this to work for lists of *any* element
52--- type, not just `Nat`? Parametric polymorphism suggests
53--- simply replacing `Nat` with a type variable `α`, but that
54--- produces a puzzling error:
55-
56-sf_expect_failure
57-  def List.elem_poly {α : Type} (a : α) (xs : List α) : Bool :=
58-    match xs with
59-    | [] => false
60-    | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_poly a tl
61-
62--- failed to synthesize instance of type class
63---   BEq α
64-
65--- Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
66-
67--- Lean is trying to use typeclasses to work out how `==`
68--- should behave on a value of type `α`. We'll see exactly why
69--- shortly; for now, here's one way to sidestep the problem:
70--- have the caller supply the equality test to use.
71-
72-def List.elem_poly_eq {α : Type} (eq : α → α → Bool) (a : α) (xs : List α) : Bool :=
73-  match xs with
74-  | [] => false
75-  | b :: tl => bif eq a b then true else elem_poly_eq eq a tl
76-
77-#eval [0, 1].elem_poly_eq Nat.beq 0
78-
79--- This works, but it's tedious: every caller has to know, and
80--- remember to supply, the right equality function.
81-
82--- Typeclasses automate this — instead of the programmer
83--- passing the function explicitly, Lean searches for one and
84--- provides it on its own. We specify something we want Lean to
85--- search for by declaring a `class` with the needed function
86--- as a field; a `class` is like an interface in Java or a
87--- trait in Rust. Particular implementations of that class are
88--- called *instance*; each type can have its own instance of a
89--- class. For functions that would use such instances, we
90--- specify the name of the class in a *instance implicit* on
91--- the polymorphic variable that the instance's function
92--- applies to. This directs Lean to rely on the class inside
93--- the function, and to find and fill in the appropriate
94--- instance when the function is called.
95-
96--- Here is what this looks like for `List.elem_poly`:
97-
98-def List.elem_poly {α : Type} [BEq α] (a : α) (xs : List α) : Bool :=
99-  match xs with
100-  | [] => false
101-  | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_poly a tl
102-
103-theorem List.elem_poly_nil {α : Type} [BEq α] (a : α) : [].elem_poly a = false := rfl
104-
105-theorem List.elem_poly_cons {α : Type} [BEq α] (a b : α) (xs : List α) :
106-    (b :: xs).elem_poly a = bif a == b then true else elem_poly a xs := rfl
107-
108-#eval [0, 1].elem_poly 0
109-
110--- Comparing `List.elem_poly_eq` with `List.elem_poly`, we see
111--- three differences. First, `List.elem_poly_eq` takes an
112--- *explicit* parameter `eq`, whereas `List.elem_poly`
113--- specifies an instance implicit `[BEq α]`. The instance
114--- implicit indicates that an instance of `BEq` must be
115--- provided at call sites for the particular type `α` that is
116--- used. Second, whereas `List.elem_poly_eq` invokes parameter
117--- `eq` to test equality, `List.elem_poly` uses `==` instead.
118--- As Lists noted when we first used it, `==` on `Nat` comes
119--- from the `BEq` typeclass. Finally, whereas
120--- `[0, 1].elem_poly_eq Nat.beq 0` passes the equality function
121--- `Nat.beq` explicitly, in `[0, 1].elem_poly 0` Lean fills it
122--- in automatically based on the type `Nat` of the `List`.
123-
124--- Note to developers (xhalo32):
125---     This is technically incorrect, the instance `BEq Nat`,
126---     which comes from `DecidableEq`, does not contain
127---     `Nat.beq`. You can see in proofs of `List.elem_nat`
128---     versus `List.elem_poly_eq` versus `List.elem_poly` and
129---     how `Nat.beq` and `==` play different roles.
130-
131--- Going back to the earlier version of `List.elem_poly`,
132--- without the instance implicit, we can now understand the
133--- error message: `α` was fully generic — so the `==` in its
134--- body would have needed to work for *every* type `α`, and no
135--- single `BEq` instance can do that. So Lean's search failed.
136-
137--- Now it is time to dig into the details of what we have seen
138--- so far. We'll see exactly how `[BEq α]` gets filled in
139--- below, starting with how to define a typeclass in the first
140--- place.
141-
142--- ## Defining Your Own Typeclasses
143-
144--- `BEq` comes from Lean's standard library. Let's define a
145--- typeclass of our own, to see the mechanism — classes,
146--- instances, and synthesis — that made `==` resolve
147--- automatically above.
148-
149--- Suppose we want a function that returns the first element of
150--- a list, defaulting to a given value if the list is empty. As
151--- with `List.elem_poly_eq` above, here is a version that makes
152--- the default value an explicit parameter:
153-
154-def List.headOr_ex {α : Type} (defaultValue : α) (xs : List α) : α :=
155-  match xs with
156-  | [] => defaultValue
157-  | hd :: _ => hd
158-
159-#eval [1, 2, 3].headOr_ex 0
160-#eval ([] : List Nat).headOr_ex 0
161-
162--- This works, but again it's tedious: every caller has to
163--- supply an element of `α` to default to, even when there's an
164--- obvious choice based on the type of the things in the list,
165--- like `0` for `Nat`.
166-
167--- Getting Lean to fill in `defaultValue` automatically takes
168--- two things. One is marking the parameter as "searchable,"
169--- rather than something the caller always supplies explicitly.
170--- The other is giving Lean some information about what it
171--- should search *for*.
172-
173--- Considering the second problem first: the way to provide
174--- this information is to *name* the data we're after — the
175--- **default value** of a type. In particular, a `structure`
176--- (chapter Lists) is a good way to give this information a
177--- name; structures can also bundle together more than one
178--- piece of data, which will come in handy later, though we
179--- only need a single field here.
180-
181--- To address the first problem, we need to mark this
182--- particular structure as one Lean should search for
183--- automatically — not every `structure`-typed argument should
184--- be.
185-
186--- Let's build up to what we want in two steps: first the
187--- naming, as a plain `structure`; then the marking, by
188--- upgrading it to a `class`. Here's the structure — we'll put
189--- it in its own namespace so we can reuse the name
190--- `DefaultValue` for the class version below:
191-
192-namespace DefaultValueScratch
193-
194-structure DefaultValue (α : Type) where
195-  value : α
196-
197--- A value of type `DefaultValue Nat` picks out a particular
198--- `Nat` to serve as the type's default: it's built the same
199--- way any structure is, by supplying a `Nat` for the `value`
200--- field:
201-
202-def natDefault : DefaultValue Nat where
203-  value := 0
204-
205-end DefaultValueScratch
206-
207--- Now for the marking: we need to tell Lean that
208--- `DefaultValue` is the sort of structure it should search for
209--- automatically, the way it needs to for `List.headOr_ex`'s
210--- `defaultValue` argument. We do this by writing `class` in
211--- place of `structure`:
212-
213-class DefaultValue (α : Type) where
214-  value : α
215-
216--- We then provide values of this type a bit differently.
217--- Instead of `def`, we use `instance`:
218-
219-instance instDefaultValueNat : DefaultValue Nat where
220-  value := 0
221-
222--- Lean can now find this instance on its own, via *typeclass
223--- synthesis* (or *typeclass inference*) — the same process
224--- that found `BEq Nat` earlier. That means we can rewrite
225--- `List.headOr_ex` the same way we rewrote `List.elem_poly_eq`
226--- into `List.elem_poly` above, replacing the explicit
227--- `defaultValue` parameter with an instance implicit:
228-
229-def List.headOr {α : Type} [DefaultValue α] (xs : List α) : α :=
230-  match xs with
231-  | [] => DefaultValue.value
232-  | hd :: _ => hd
233-
234-#eval [1, 2, 3].headOr
235-#eval ([] : List Nat).headOr
236-
237-example : DefaultValue.value = (0 : Nat) := by rfl
238-
239--- Notice that we refer to `DefaultValue.value` alone, with no
240--- instance named. Because the expression equates
241--- `DefaultValue.value` with the `Nat` `0`, Lean selects
242--- `instDefaultValueNat`, the instance for `DefaultValue Nat`.
243--- We know this because we are able to prove that
244--- `DefaultValue.value` is equal to `0`.
245-
246--- Let's declare a second instance, for `Int`, the type of
247--- integers `... -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, ...`:
248-
249-instance instDefaultValueInt : DefaultValue Int where
250-  value := -1
251-
252--- We can also create instances for polymorphic types, like
253--- `Option α`, whose default is `none`, by giving the instance
254--- declaration a parameter:
255-
256-instance instDefaultValueOption {α : Type} : DefaultValue (Option α) where
257-  value := none
258-
259--- Now, Lean can infer instances for all these types, including
260--- inside `List.headOr`:
261-
262-example : DefaultValue.value = (0 : Nat) := by rfl
263-example : DefaultValue.value = (-1 : Int) := by rfl
264-example : DefaultValue.value = (none : Option Bool) := by rfl
265-example : DefaultValue.value = (none : Option (List Nat)) := by rfl
266-example : ([] : List Nat).headOr = 0 := by rfl
267-example : ([] : List Int).headOr = -1 := by rfl
268-example : ([] : List (Option Bool)).headOr = none := by rfl
269-example : ([] : List (Option Bool)).headOr = none := by rfl
270-
271--- Synthesis infers instances we could have specified
272--- explicitly:
273-
274-example : instDefaultValueNat.value = (0 : Nat) := by rfl
275-example : instDefaultValueInt.value = (-1 : Int) := by rfl
276-example : instDefaultValueOption.value = (none : Option Nat) := by rfl
277-
278--- The option `pp.all` shows which instance Lean picked:
279-
280-set_option pp.all true in
281-#check (DefaultValue.value : Nat)
282-
283--- @DefaultValue.value Nat instDefaultValueNat : Nat
284-
285-set_option pp.all true in
286-#check (DefaultValue.value : Int)
287-
288--- @DefaultValue.value Int instDefaultValueInt : Int
289-
290--- This reveals `instDefaultValueNat` and `instDefaultValueInt`
291--- as the instances Lean picked. The `#synth` command runs the
292--- same search directly:
293-
294-#synth DefaultValue Nat
295-
296--- instDefaultValueNat
297-
298--- For a typeclass like `DefaultValue` that carries data — a
299--- term, such as the `1` above, rather than only proofs (which
300--- we will see below) — we expect at most one instance per
301--- type, so this search has a unique answer.
302-
303--- We'll put `DefaultValue`'s standard-library equivalent,
304--- `Inhabited`, to work later in this chapter, when we define
305--- maps that need a default value for a generic type. First,
306--- though, let's go back to `List.elem_poly` and see how its
307--- `[BEq α]` argument actually gets resolved.
308-
309--- ## Using Typeclasses
310-
311--- Let's check what `==` meant for `List.elem_nat`, with
312--- notation display turned off:
313-
314-set_option pp.notation false in
315-#check 1 == 2
316-
317--- BEq.beq 1 2 : Bool
318-
319--- Rather than `Nat.beq`, `==` turns out to be notation for
320--- `BEq.beq`, a field of exactly the kind of typeclass we just
321--- learned to define:
322-
323-sf_recall_source
324-  /--
325-    `BEq α` is a typeclass for supplying a boolean-valued equality relation on
326-    `α`, notated as `a == b`. Unlike `DecidableEq α` (which uses `a = b`), this
327-    is `Bool` valued instead of `Prop` valued, and it also does not have any
328-    axioms like being reflexive or agreeing with `=`. It is mainly intended for
329-    programming applications. See `LawfulBEq` for a version that requires that
330-    `==` and `=` coincide.
331-  
332-    Typically we prefer to put the "more variable" term on the left,
333-    and the "more constant" term on the right.
334-    -/
335-    class BEq (α : Type u) where
336-      /-- Boolean equality, notated as `a == b`. -/
337-      beq : α → α → Bool
338-
339--- Writing `a == b` makes Lean search for an **instance** of
340--- `BEq` for the type of `a` and `b`, the same way it searched
341--- for a `DefaultValue` instance above. For `Nat`, that
342--- instance is:
343-
344-instance (priority := low) : BEq Nat where
345-  beq := Nat.beq
346-
347--- This is the instance Lean supplies for `[BEq α]` when
348--- `List.elem_poly` is called on a `List Nat` — no different
349--- from Lean choosing `instDefaultValueNat` for
350--- `DefaultValue.value` earlier when it was equated with
351--- `(1 : Nat)`.
352-
353--- ### Exercise (1 star): List.elem_poly_eq_elem_nat ⭐
354-
355--- Prove that `List.elem_poly` agrees with `List.elem_nat` when
356--- specialized to natural numbers.
357-
358-theorem List.elem_poly_eq_elem_nat (xs : List Nat) (n : Nat) : xs.elem_poly n = xs.elem_nat n := by
359-  sorry

361--- ## Proof-Carrying Typeclasses
362-
363--- The above examples enforce no conditions on the data an
364--- instance may carry — any value of the right type will do.
365--- But sometimes enforcing constraints on data is useful. For
366--- example, suppose we want to specify that a type has not just
367--- a single element, but two. Here is a first attempt:
368-
369-sf_experiment
370-  class HasTwoIncomplete (α : Type) where
371-    one : α
372-    two : α
373-
374--- Unfortunately, this specification isn't precise because it
375--- allows `one` and `two` to refer to the same term.
376--- Fortunately, Lean's typeclasses can carry proofs along with
377--- data, so we can write the following to enforce that `one`
378--- and `two` are distinct.
379-
380-class HasTwo (α : Type) where
381-  one : α
382-  two : α
383-  one_neq_two : one ≠ two
384-
385--- Declaring instances works in much the same way as before,
386--- except that now the `HasTwo.one_neq_two` field requires a
387--- proof:
388-
389-instance : HasTwo Nat where
390-  one := 1
391-  two := 2
392-  one_neq_two := by intro contra; contradiction
393-
394--- In most languages that support typeclasses (or traits) it is
395--- not possible to formally enforce laws such as `one_neq_two`.
396--- Thus it falls to the author to check, informally, that any
397--- required invariants are satisfied, which can lead to bugs.
398-
399--- ### Exercise (1 star): HasThree ⭐
400-
401--- Following the pattern of `DefaultValue` and `HasTwo`, define
402--- a class `HasThree` that specifies a type with at least three
403--- distinct elements, and give an instance of it for `Nat`.
404-
405-class HasThree (α : Type) where
406-  one : α
407-  two : α
408-  three : α
409-  one_neq_two : one ≠ two
410-  -- FILL IN HERE
411-
412-instance : HasThree Nat where
413-  one := 1
414-  two := 2
415-  three := 3
416-  one_neq_two := sorry
417-  -- FILL IN HERE
418-
419-namespace Algebra
420-
421--- This facility is very powerful, and is used extensively in
422--- Lean to define mathematical structures that carry both
423--- operators and laws about how those operators interact. As a
424--- simple example, let's use a typeclass to define a *monoid*,
425--- a simple algebraic structure that includes four things:
426-
427--- - an underlying set of data, represented by a type `α`,
428-
429--- - an operator (which we'll write `⊗`, typed otimes) that
430---   combines two elements of type `α` into one,
431-
432--- - a particular element `id` of type `α`, which we call the
433---   "identity element", and
434-
435--- - some laws about the interaction of `⊗` and `id`, namely
436---   that:
437-
438---   - `∀ x, id ⊗ x = x = x ⊗ id`, and
439-
440---   - `∀ x y z, x ⊗ (y ⊗ z) = (x ⊗ y) ⊗ z` (i.e., that `⊗` is
441---     associative)
442-
443--- We can express these requirements in the form of a
444--- typeclass:
445-
446--- first we define a notation typeclass for our operator ⊗
447-class OpSet (α : Type) where
448-  op : α → α → α
449-
450-infixr:70 " ⊗ " => OpSet.op
451-
452-class Monoid (α : Type) extends (OpSet α) where
453-  id : α
454-  left_id : ∀ (x : α), id ⊗ x = x
455-  right_id : ∀ (x : α), x ⊗ id = x
456-  assoc : ∀ (x y z : α), x ⊗ (y ⊗ z) = (x ⊗ y) ⊗ z
457-
458--- The `extends` keyword indicates that the `Monoid` typeclass
459--- extends the `OpSet` typeclass, which just defines a set with
460--- an operator and some notation for it. The `Monoid` typeclass
461--- "inherits" the fields of `OpSet`, similar to how a class
462--- would in an object-oriented language.
463-
464--- As one might expect, the `+` operator over `Nat`s forms a
465--- monoid, where `0` is the identity element. Note that we
466--- don't have to define `Nat`'s `OpSet` instance separately, we
467--- can define a single instance that implements both classes.
468-
469-instance : Monoid Nat where
470-  op := Nat.add
471-  id := 0
472-  left_id := by lia
473-  right_id := by lia
474-  assoc := by lia
475-
476--- ### Exercise (1 star): NatMonoidMul ⭐
477-
478--- However, multiplication on `Nat`s *also* forms a monoid.
479--- What is its identity element?
480-
481-instance : Monoid Nat where
482-  op := Nat.mul
483-  id := sorry
484-  left_id := sorry
485-  right_id := sorry
486-  assoc := sorry
487-
488--- ### Exercise (1 star): ListMonoidAppend ⭐
489-
490--- There are also many monoids over other types. Most usefully
491--- in computer science, lists of any type also form a monoid,
492--- with `List.append` as the operator in question:
493-
494-instance {α : Type} : Monoid (List α) where
495-  op := List.append
496-  id := sorry
497-  left_id := sorry
498-  right_id := sorry
499-  assoc := sorry
500-
501--- In addition to defining instances of `Monoid`, we can also
502--- prove some properties about monoids in general, just based
503--- on the laws defined on the typeclass. One simple theorem
504--- about monoids is that the identity element of a monoid is
505--- unique. That is, if we have two monoids over the same set
506--- with the same operator, their identity elements must also be
507--- the same:
508-
509-theorem id_unique {α : Type} {m₁ m₂ : Monoid α} (h : m₁.op = m₂.op) : m₁.id = m₂.id := by
510-  obtain @⟨op₁, id₁, left_id₁, right_id₁, assoc₁⟩ := m₁
511-  obtain @⟨op₂, id₂, left_id₂, right_id₂, assoc₂⟩ := m₂
512-  have h' : id₁ = id₂ := by
513-    -- this introduces a use of m₁'s operator
514-    rw [← left_id₁ id₂]
515-    -- we use our hypothesis to rewrite m₁'s operator into m₂'s
516-    rw [h]
517-    -- then, we can use m₂'s right id
518-    rw [right_id₂]
519-  -- the goal `m₁.id = m₂.id` is equivalent with `id₁ = id₂` even though it displays `Monoid.id = Monoid.id`
520-  exact h'
521-
522--- In the above proof, we can destructure the monoid instances
523--- `m₁` and `m₂` with the `obtain` tactic we saw in the Logic
524--- chapter. When we do so however, because these are class
525--- instances instead of normal structures, we preface our tuple
526--- with the `@` symbol. When stepping through the above proof,
527--- if the notation is confusing to you, remember that you can
528--- set `set_option pp.all true` or
529--- `set_option pp.explicit true` to make Lean show you more
530--- clearly what is going on. For example, the goal is displayed
531--- as `Monoid.id = Monoid.id` since the instances `m₁` and `m₂`
532--- are implicit arguments to `Monoid.id`. Setting
533--- `pp.explicit true` displays the goal as
534--- `@Eq α (@Monoid.id α m₁) (@Monoid.id α m₂)`.
535-
536--- A *group* is a special kind of monoid with an *inverse*
537--- operation `inv`, which has the property that
538--- `∀ x, inv x ⊗ x = id = x ⊗ inv x`. We can extend the
539--- definition of a `Monoid` to capture this new feature:
540-
541-class Group (α : Type) extends (Monoid α) where
542-  inv : α → α
543-  left_inv : ∀ (x : α), inv x ⊗ x = id
544-  right_inv: ∀ (x : α), x ⊗ inv x = id
545-
546--- Now, the monoids we described earlier are not groups: there
547--- is no inverse operation on the natural numbers such that
548--- `∀ x, x + inv x = 0 = inv x + x`, for example. However,
549--- addition does form a group over the integers:
550-
551--- ### Exercise (1 star): IntGroupAdd ⭐
552-
553-instance : Group Int where
554-  op := Int.add
555-  id := sorry
556-  inv := sorry
557-  left_id := sorry
558-  right_id := sorry
559-  assoc := sorry
560-  left_inv := sorry
561-  right_inv := sorry
562-
563--- The study of groups is called *group theory* and is a rich
564--- area of mathematics. Here, we will only prove a handful of
565--- its simplest results:
566-
567--- Note to developers (Daniel Sainati @dsainati1):
568---     This also prints weird.
569-
570--- ### Exercise (1 star): InverseUnique ⭐
571-
572--- Two groups defined with the same operation over the same set
573--- must have the same inverse as well.
574-
575-theorem inv_unique {α : Type} {g₁ g₂ : Group α} (h : g₁.op = g₂.op) : g₁.inv = g₂.inv := by
576-  sorry
577-
578--- Note to developers (Daniel Sainati @dsainati1):
579---     Taking suggestions for additional simple group theory
580---     theorems to prove here.
581-
582-end Algebra
583-
584--- ## Maps
585-
586--- *Maps* (or "dictionaries") are ubiquitous data structures
587--- both in ordinary programming and in the theory of
588--- programming languages; we're going to need them in many
589--- places in later volumes.
590-
591--- We'll define two flavors of maps: *total maps*, which
592--- include a "default" element to be returned when a key being
593--- looked up doesn't exist, and *partial maps*, which instead
594--- return an option to indicate success or failure. Partial
595--- maps are defined in terms of total maps, using `none` as the
596--- default element.
597-
598--- ### Key and Value Types
599-
600--- To define maps, we first need a type for the keys that we
601--- will use to index into our maps and a type for the values
602--- the maps return. In this section, we'll use the type
603--- variable `α` for the type of keys and `β` for values. In
604--- addition to `BEq`, which we have already seen, our key type
605--- `α` requires instances of the `ReflBEq` and `LawfulBEq`
606--- typeclasses:
607-
608-sf_recall_source
609-  /-- `ReflBEq α` says that the `BEq` implementation is reflexive. -/
610-    class ReflBEq (α) [BEq α] : Prop where
611-      /-- `==` is reflexive, that is, `(a == a) = true`. -/
612-      protected rfl {a : α} : a == a
613-
614-sf_recall_source
615-  /--
616-    A Boolean equality test coincides with propositional equality.
617-  
618-    In other words:
619-     * `a == b` implies `a = b`.
620-     * `a == a` is true.
621-    -/
622-    class LawfulBEq (α : Type u) [BEq α] : Prop extends ReflBEq α where
623-      /-- If `a == b` evaluates to `true`, then `a` and `b` are equal in the logic. -/
624-      eq_of_beq : {a b : α} → a == b → a = b
625-
626--- These classes refine `BEq`, specifying that (`==`) is
627--- reflexive and coincides with proposition equality `=`.
628-
629--- In general, we place no constraints on the value type `β`.
630-
631--- ### Total Maps
632-
633--- The Lists chapter introduced a partial map abstraction,
634--- `PartialMap`, with a `find` function for lookup, based on
635--- lists of key-value pairs. Here, we are going to build a map
636--- abstraction using functions instead. The advantage of this
637--- representation is that it offers a more *extensional* view
638--- of maps, as we saw with functions in the Logic chapter: two
639--- maps that respond to every query in the same way will be
640--- represented as exactly the same function, rather than just
641--- as "equivalent" list structures. This simplifies proofs that
642--- use maps.
643-
644--- Instead of using functions directly, we encapsulate them
645--- inside a `structure` which we call `TotalMap`. Intuitively,
646--- a total map just contains a function `inner` from a key of
647--- type `α` to a value of type `β`.
648-
649-structure TotalMap (α : Type) (β : Type) where
650-  inner : α → β
651-
652-namespace TotalMap
653-
654--- In order to declare a default value of `β` we will use the
655--- `Inhabited` typeclass, which is the standard library's
656--- implementation of our `DefaultValue` example from above:
657-
658--- The function `TotalMap.empty` yields an empty total map,
659--- given a default element; this map always returns the default
660--- element when applied to any key.
661-
662-def empty {α β : Type} [Inhabited β] : TotalMap α β where
663-  inner := fun _ ↦ default
664-
665--- These types and implicit instances are now available
666--- automatically to all the definitions in this section.
667-
668--- Just as declaring `BEq`/`DefaultValue` instances above
669--- hooked `==` and `DefaultValue.value` up to our types, we can
670--- declare an instance of the standard library's
671--- `EmptyCollection` typeclass to associate `∅` with this empty
672--- map.
673-
674-instance {α β : Type} [Inhabited β] : EmptyCollection (TotalMap α β) where
675-  emptyCollection := TotalMap.empty
676-
677-theorem empty_def {α β : Type} [Inhabited β] : (∅ : TotalMap α β) = { inner := fun _ ↦ default } := by rfl
678-
679--- Here, for example, is an empty map that takes `Nat` keys to
680--- `Nat` values:
681-
682-def emptyNatMap : TotalMap Nat Nat := ∅
683-
684--- #### Getting Elements
685-
686--- While `TotalMap`s happen to be implemented as functions
687--- under the hood, we would prefer not to expose this fact in
688--- its public interface. Accordingly, we define new operations
689--- for querying and updating mappings. We define a function
690--- `get` for getting the value associated with a key playing
691--- the role that `find` played for the Lists chapter's
692--- list-based maps,
693-
694-def get {α β : Type} (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) := m.inner a
695-
696-/-- This exposes implementation-specific details of `TotalMap`.
697-Avoid using this outside the `TotalMap` namespace. -/
698-theorem get_def {α β : Type} {m : TotalMap α β} {a : α} : m.get a = m.inner a := by rfl
699-
700-example : emptyNatMap.get 2 = 0 := by rfl
701-
702--- Here is an example that uses the API lemmas `empty_def` and
703--- `get_def`:
704-
705-example {n : Nat} : emptyNatMap.get n = 0 := by
706-  rewrite [get_def, emptyNatMap, empty_def, Nat.default_eq_zero]
707-  rfl
708-
709--- In the above example, we use `rewrite` and `rfl` instead of
710--- the usual `rw` to highlight something interesting. After the
711--- rewrites in this proof, we end up with a goal that looks
712--- like `{ inner := fun x => 0 }.inner n = 0`, which we can
713--- solve with `rfl`. This is because the projection `.inner` on
714--- a structure of the form `{ inner := x }` is definitionally
715--- equal to `x`.
716-
717--- `get` is the public API counterpart to `inner` which is an
718--- implementation-specific detail of `TotalMap`. Because
719--- `get_def` "peeks" through the abstraction, it should be used
720--- sparingly, and only inside the `TotalMap` namespace.
721-
722--- To make element-getting more convenient, let's define
723--- notation so we can write `emptyNatMap[2]` rather than
724--- `emptyNatMap.get`. We could notate `get` directly — we'll do
725--- exactly that for `update` below — but here we'll instead
726--- make "getting an element" its own typeclass, `MyGetElem`,
727--- and notate it. Doing so means `m[a]` resolves to
728--- `MyGetElem.getElem m a` for any type with a `MyGetElem`
729--- instance, not just `TotalMap`.
730-
731--- Using typeclasses to define notation is typical in Lean when
732--- the same notation is useful for many different types. We
733--- have seen the approach already with `==`: writing `a == b`
734--- is notation for `BEq.beq`, resolved by instance search for
735--- whatever type `a` and `b` have. We also just saw overloaded
736--- notation for `EmptyCollection` above, where `∅` is notation
737--- for `EmptyCollection.emptyCollection`. Our typeclass
738--- `MyGetElem` is a simpler version of the standard library's
739--- `GetElem` typeclass, which has many instances such as
740--- `Array`, `List`, and `Vector`. We develop it to illustrate
741--- the notation-as-typeclass approach.
742-
743--- Note to developers (Niklas Halonen @xhalo32):
744---     A reason I can come up with why we use a notation
745---     typeclass (in library code) over a plain notation is
746---     that it makes it possible (for a downstream consumer) to
747---     write `open scoped MyGetElem` instead of writing
748---     `open scoped TotalMap` and `open scoped PartialMap`
749---     individually. This wouldn't be a good sell if `→ₜ` and
750---     `→ₚ` are scoped notations, but they're currently global.
751-
752-end TotalMap
753-
754--- The `MyGetElem` typeclass takes three type parameters: the
755--- map implementation, its keys, and its values.
756-
757-class MyGetElem (coll : Type) (idx : Type) (elem : outParam Type) where
758-  getElem (xs : coll) (i : idx) : elem
759-
760--- (Don't worry about the `outParam` qualifier; it is a hint to
761--- Lean that helps typeclass inference.)
762-
763--- The appropriate instance of `MyGetElem` for our `TotalMap`
764--- is:
765-
766-instance {α β : Type} : MyGetElem (TotalMap α β) α β where

836--- #### Updating Elements
837-
838--- Now we turn to the `update` function, which takes a map `m`,
839--- a key `a`, and a value `b` and returns a new map that takes
840--- `a` to `b` and takes every other key to whatever `m` does.
841--- We do this by wrapping a new map function around the old
842--- one.
843-
844-def update {α β : Type} (m : TotalMap α β) [BEq α] (a : α) (b : β) : TotalMap α β where
845-  inner := fun a' => bif a == a' then b else m[a']
846-
847--- For example, we can build a map taking `String` to `Bool`,
848--- where `"foo"` and `"bar"` are mapped to `true` and every
849--- other key is mapped to `false`, like this:
850-
851-def exampleMap :=
852-  (∅ : TotalMap String Bool)
853-    |>.update "foo" true
854-    |>.update "bar" true
855-
856--- Here `|>` is Lean's **pipe** notation: `x |>.f y` means
857--- `x.f y`, letting us chain a sequence of function or method
858--- calls left to right without nested parentheses.
859-
860--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):

862---     good places to use it earlier?)

864--- We also introduce a notation for updating maps — this time,
865--- rather than going through a typeclass and its own
866--- `notation`/`macro_rules` machinery as we did for
867--- `MyGetElem`, we write a `notation` that references
868--- `TotalMap.update` directly. Unlike indexing, `update`
869--- doesn't need to work generically across container types
870--- (there's no standard-library operation like `GetElem` that
871--- we're mirroring here), so the simpler, direct route
872--- suffices.
873-
874-notation a:55 " →ₜ " b:55 " ; " m:55 => TotalMap.update m a b
875-
876-/-- This exposes implementation-specific details of `TotalMap`.
877-Avoid using this outside the `TotalMap` namespace. Prefer `update_apply` if possible. -/
878-theorem update_def {α β : Type} [BEq α] (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) (b : β) :
879-  a →ₜ b ; m = { inner := fun a' => bif a == a' then b else m[a'] } := by rfl
880-
881-theorem update_apply {α β : Type} [BEq α] (m : TotalMap α β) (a a' : α) (b : β) :
882-  (a →ₜ b ; m)[a'] = bif a == a' then b else m[a'] := by rfl

887-notation a:55 " →ₜ " b:55 => TotalMap.update ∅ a b

1100--- ### Notation for Concrete Maps
1101-
1102--- Wouldn't it be nice if we could use a more natural notation
1103--- for concrete maps like `{ "bar" ↦ true, "foo" ↦ true }`? To
1104--- accomplish this we define a simple structure that consists
1105--- of a key and a value along with `↦` notation for it.
1106-
1107-/--
1108-A key-value pair with `↦` syntax.
1109--/
1110-@[ext]
1111-structure KVPair (K : Type) (V : Type) where
1112-  key : K
1113-  value : V
1114-
1115-namespace KVPair
1116-scoped notation k " ↦ " v => KVPair.mk k v
1117-end KVPair
1118-
1119-open scoped KVPair
1120-
1121--- Next, we declare `Insert` and `Singleton` instances — the
1122--- standard-library typeclasses behind the `{x, y, ...}` and
1123--- `{x}` collection-literal notation that `List`, `Finset`, and
1124--- other stdlib containers already support — so that `TotalMap`
1125--- can use it too.
1126-
1127-namespace TotalMap
1128-
1129-instance {α β : Type} [BEq α] : Insert (KVPair α β) (TotalMap α β) where
1130-  insert kv m := kv.key →ₜ kv.value ; m
1131-
1132-instance {α β : Type} [BEq α] [Inhabited β] : Singleton (KVPair α β) (TotalMap α β) where
1133-  singleton kv := insert kv ∅
1134-
1135-instance {α β : Type} [BEq α] [Inhabited β] : LawfulSingleton (KVPair α β) (TotalMap α β) where
1136-  insert_empty_eq _ := rfl
1137-
1138-end TotalMap

1177--- Lastly, we define *partial maps* on top of total maps. A
1178--- partial map with elements of type `β` is simply a total map
1179--- with elements of type `Option β`, whose default element is
1180--- `none`.

1182-structure PartialMap (α : Type) (β : Type) where
1183-  /-- The underlying total map. Lean always generates a public projection for a structure
1184-  field, so `inner` is technically accessible, but it isn't part of the intended interface:
1185-  use `PartialMap.toTotal` instead, so there's exactly one sanctioned way to get at it. -/
1186-  inner : TotalMap α (Option β)
1187-
1188-/- Note that this definition of `EmptyCollection` doesn't need `β` to have an `Inhabited` instance
1189-   like `TotalMap` did. This is because `Option β` has its own `Inhabited` instance: `none` is a value
1190-   of every `Option` type. -/

1192-  emptyCollection := { inner := ∅ }

1233--- Updating a partial map at a key means storing a `some` value

1385--- In this section, we will make use of some definitions and
1386--- theorems about natural numbers that we discussed and proved
1387--- in previous chapters; copy your solutions to those problems
1388--- here:
1389-
1390-namespace Nat
1391-

1393-  match n with
1394-  | 0     => true
1395-  | 1     => false
1396-  | n + 2 => even n
1397-
1398-theorem even_zero : even 0 = true := by rfl
1399-

1401-    even (n + 1) = !(even n) := by
1402-  sorry
1403-
1404-def double (n : Nat) : Nat :=
1405-  match n with
1406-  | 0    => 0
1407-  | n' + 1 => double n' + 2

1409-theorem double_zero : double 0 = 0 := by rfl
1410-
1411-theorem double_succ (n : Nat) : double (n + 1) = double n + 2 := by rfl
1412-
1413-def Even x := ∃ n : Nat, x = Nat.double n
